Queen's Domain review

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's tempting to begin with King's Field; after all, FromSoftware's seminal first-person action-RPG is an explicit inspiration for developer Freshly Baked Games.
  • Industry observers note that all this begins with an island.
  • There is so much to say about Neasied.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Where to start with Queen's Domain? It's tempting to begin with King's Field; after all, FromSoftware's seminal first-person action-RPG is an explicit inspiration for developer Freshly Baked Games. But 40 hours later, it feels like so much more. It's equally tempting to invoke another FromSoftware game: Dark Souls. Queen's Domain owes an obvious debt to that game's celebrated level design: the dazzling interconnectedness of its vertiginous world. But that's not quite right either. The deeper you delve, the more there's something of the spirit of The Legend of Zelda, a touch of Metroidvania too. Until finally you concede that Queen's Domain, with its remarkable world of densely packed secrets, is very much its own.

Industry observers note that all this begins with an island. You, Prince Beruim, are a castaway, washed ashore on Neasied. Your father, the king, has disappeared, and your search has brought you, somewhat circuitously, here. As you clamber to your feet and survey the island, it makes an immediately striking impression: all strange peaks and crooked spires; a cramped, chaotic mass of landmarks lost amid the dense undergrowth. Pyramids perch atop steep plateaus; a vast, moss-tinged mausoleum sprawls across the land to one side while the other is dominated by an imposing tower. It's a world made all the stranger by Queen's Domain's retro aesthetic. Here, shimmering low-res textures and low-poly shapes converge to create elaborate spaces and structures that feel slightly at odds with the lo-fi vibe. It's not quite old, not quite new; instead, something of a world lost outside of time. It makes for an enigmatic, disorientating landscape. And when paired with a soundtrack that delights in discordance, as it swings from gentle ambience to pulsing synths, it's a mood that refuses to resolve.

There is so much to say about Neasied. And so much I absolutely will not spoil. But very early impressions don't do it justice at all. As you take your first tentative steps onto the island, presented with a forking path that eventually winds back in on itself, it's easy to mistake Queen's Domain for a first-person Dark Souls - especially if, like me, you're only passingly familiar with King's Field. As in most Soulslikes, early progress is defined by a punishing inch-by-inch crawl from one brutal encounter to the next; where death - via chicken-cricket hybrids, ladybird-rats, and other wonderfully odd things - comes fast and frequently, respawning you back at the last Crystal Monument you visited. And because its wilfully old-school design eschews modern-day niceties such as a combat lock-on or dedicated roll button, there's a looseness to fighting that takes a while to click. But it does, slowly, click.

This is a game that demands you lean into its limitations, encourages you to find ways to make them work. At first, those Souls-honed instincts are likely to be your undoing as you naturally scramble for a dodge button that isn't there. But soon a different sort of pattern emerges: you realise that to avoid a ladybird attack, you simply need to step back - but not so far you don't have time to nip in and strike while your opponent takes a pause. A charging enemy might require a different approach - a well-timed backstep and swivelling sideways strafe to put you in the right place for a counter. And in this way, combat becomes a compelling sort of puzzle as you learn each of the 100+ enemies' little ticks - including rock, paper, scissors-style weaknesses to different weapon types - and figure out how to respond.

There's more to consider. Your melee damage output, for instance, is directly tied to your stamina bar: the more stamina you have, the harder you'll hit; too low and it's a waste of a swing. That forces you to choose your moments carefully, moving out to safety while your bar refills. And there's a charge attack, also linked to your stamina, that does more damage still. Already combat has a distinctively deliberate rhythm, but then come your first throwing knives. These are most immediately useful against enemies ordinarily out of reach - like the laser-spewing foliage dogging your journey early on - but they're equally valuable for luring individual enemies away from the throng. Throwing weapons take a while to return to your pouch, meaning they too need to be deployed with purpose. And while knives are just the start - you'll acquire an increasingly exotic selection of throwables including poison-tipped darts and homing blades - they all fundamentally work the same way.

It has been revealed that and the interplay of these various warm-ups and cooldowns creates an increasingly engaging rhythm as you learn to juggle between your variously equipped weapons to maximise their damage potential. You might, for instance, fire off a one-two-three volley of homing darts, then use a magic lantern to toss out a massive fireball that bounces destructively around the room. And it's there, in the ensuing chaos, you'll charge up your blade, letting rip then returning to your darts again. Combat might encourage a methodical pace, but that doesn't mean you can't fight fast, and there are some fascinating synergies among the various weapons, many having their own wonderfully distinct mechanisms. There's a brawling gauntlet that lifts you clean off the ground and a vampiric blade capable of stealing an enemy's life force. There are hammers, creatures, and an unexpected mid-game weapon class, utilising a third rechargeable power source, that I am definitely not spoiling. Queen's Domain's 100 or so weapons create ample space for experimentation and customisation, and the further from its cautious beginnings you stray, the brisker, the more exhilarating its combat becomes. In my current, late-game form, I'm a whirl of blades and blasts and up-close attacks that feels anything but Soulslike.

According to recent reports, queen's Domain isn't just a nippier sort of game, though. It promptly reveals itself to be friendlier, more accommodating. Levelling, for instance, happens passively as you play, meaning every swing feels like it's contributing to your progress. Weapons level independently too, encouraging specialisation. There are no flasks, no accumulated currency you'll need to worry about dropping on death, no subsequent corpse runs. And progress can be saved at any time using the nearest Crystal Monument, meaning that when you respawn, you won't have to grind through the same opponents again. Enemies do eventually reappear of their own accord, so you can't exploit the save system indefinitely. But unlike Souls-style bonfires, Crystal Monuments only repopulate the world when you explicitly tell them to - when you Rest to clear status effects and restore health - giving you considerably more agency. You can decide when to push forward, when to retreat and lock in your progress, and when to reap the benefits of a rest and reset. Together, it makes for a breezier, less punishing, more consistently rewarding riff on the traditional Souslike, while never losing that I-can-do-this just-one-more-turn allure.

But as immensely enjoyable as Queen's Domain's combat is, the real draw here, unquestionably, is the world. Neasied is extraordinary. Right from the start, as you pick yourself off the sand and survey the landscape, its enigmatic huddle of peculiar landmarks isn't just intriguing, it's inviting. These odd pyramids, these curious plateaus practically demand to be explored. But how? The answer comes perhaps an hour in when, fancily clad skeleton boss successfully slain, you get your hands on the Holy Sword Endu. It's an immediate boon, far more lethal than the rubbish rusty blade you've been wielding so far. And its secondary attack - a long-range jab that propels you forward - is handy too. It's also your key to unlocking Neasied.

It has been revealed that endu's violent forward momentum can, you see, fling you across previously uncrossable gaps, gradually carrying you further and further as more upgrades reveal themselves. Suddenly, Queen's Domain takes flight, quite literally, becoming something closer to an exploratory sandbox as it adopts the spirited acrobatics of a platform game. And as you experiment with your newfound freedom, the more paths you explore, the island begins to take on a dizzying new form. Neasied, when viewed from up high, reveals itself to be a vastly intricate traversal puzzle. That peculiar structure in the distance? If you can find an appropriate ledge to fling yourself from, it's now yours for the investigating - and from there, one, two, three more tantalising branches are revealed. Neasied is an astonishing piece of design: a ludicrous, elaborate tangle of hidden pathways and secrets, forever folding in and around itself, that's crafted to invite curiosity and then constantly reward.

Sources indicate that freshly Baked Games always feels one step ahead. I can't recall a single moment where my exploratory What-ifs - What if I throw myself this way? What if I do a falling mid-air turn? What if I toss myself down this hole? - didn't bear fruit. Sometimes your prize is a steaming platter of boon-granting food, sometimes it's another bit of increasingly exotic weaponry. Perhaps you'll find a strange NPC with a favour to ask; fish eggs and mysterious skulls; a shopkeeper with a thing for ducks (who, in a typically lovely touch, festoons his store with the goods you're willing to sell), and so many mysterious upcoming puzzle threads to pull. As you fling and probe and push on forward, that thing you've been carrying around for hours - or, conversely, that thing you saw hours ago - suddenly finds new purpose. There's a definite touch of Metroidvania as old areas reveal new truths the further you go. And because there's so little handholding, so little explicit direction, every discovery feels like your own.

But just as you think you're starting to get a handle on Queen's Domain's shape, along comes another surprise: dungeons as vastly intricate as the world outside. You'll navigate labyrinthine waterlogged caverns of angry fish where progress involves puzzling past ancient mechanisms. Later, an arcane tower where gargoyles prowl. Here, the convoluted upward route takes circuitous laps among the endless bookshelves, spilling out the windows onto teetering precipices with alarming sea views. Then down, however briefly, to eerie chambers below. Suddenly, the mood is less Soulslike, more Zelda, and your expectations shift again. And still new discoveries lead to new paths and fresh mysteries.

According to recent reports, and it keeps on going. As Freshly Baked Games gradually peels back Neasied's layers, it constantly finds new ways to awe: yet more surprises, yet more secrets, your exploratory digressions earning still more intriguing rewards. There comes a point where you think surely you must have seen everything, explored its deepest caverns and most mysterious tombs, but down you go again. And somewhere around the midpoint, Queen's Domain takes a truly audacious turn. There is a - let's call it a tonal lurch for fear of spoilers - that signals another shift. Suddenly, there are new toys to play with, an autumnal landscape so complex in its demands, it genuinely made my brain pulse. And then it's over. Until it's not.

There are, it turns out, secrets beneath the secrets; a still more intricate web of interconnected threads spun throughout this already fascinating, impossibly complex world. The Neasied that welcomes you really is just the tip of it all. Exactly when you'll come to this realisation depends how thorough you are in the earlier hours - how willing you are to explore its darker corners and brave its more punishing realms - but for me the before-and-after managed to divide my 40-ish hour playthrough neatly in two. You reawaken with a sense of a quest unfulfilled, a hint that more is required. And so, in lieu of more explicit direction, you set out again, probe deeper, explore further, and slowly the vaguest shape of a latest objective - a succession of tiny threads seemingly all leading in the same direction - begins to emerge. Tucked along uncharted paths, perhaps, or in suspicious corners, or in item descriptions that suddenly feels like clues.

It's here in this second half - something of a dark mirror to the first, in classic Zelda style - that Queen's Domain takes on a more esoteric air; its web of distantly scattered enigmas requiring real dedication to unfurl. Why this pot on a stick? Why this book? How do these unlit lanterns relate to this thing, and that thing, and this other thing on the other side of the world?

It's clever stuff, even if navigating its late-game threads can occasionally feel just a little too much, a little too abstruse, and you'll potentially face a lot of needle-in-a-haystack backtracking if you haven't been taking judicious notes as you go. Do I have any other quibbles? There are perhaps too few boss encounters that feel like genuine events. And while combat generally feels fair and balanced, serving as a propulsive drumbeat to the broader exploratory rhythms, there are a few late-game all-the-enemies-at-once-style difficulty spikes that go just a bit too far. But then another 'What if?' and the world responds, and those frustrations melt away.

It has been revealed that I remember a time in my youth - back before dataminers and FAQs - when video games felt unknowable. Endless enigmas built from creativity and code. It felt like anything could be hiding in there if only you knew where to look, and it was easy to let your imagination run wild. Queen's Domain is so full of secrets, so full of mystery and wonder, it feels like the sort of game my enthusiastic child-brain might have dreamed up all those years ago. 40 hours in, I've seen an ending, but it feels like I'm still far from through. So many mysteries still linger, so many things remain on my checklist of speculative to-dos. Out in the real-world, I've got a Zelda and a GTA awaiting. But it says everything about Queen's Domain - this brilliant, vast, deep enigma; this absurdly audacious thing - that I'm still not yet ready to let go.

A copy of Queen's Domain was provided for this review by Future Friends Games.

#172323. People are taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. AI found something surprising

📅 22 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1453 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

People are taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. AI found something surprising

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1453 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that an experimental weight-loss drug that has not yet received regulatory approval is already attracting users willing to obtain unapproved versions online.
  • Recent findings suggest that the drug, retatrutide, belongs to a upcoming generation of GLP-1 medications designed to help regulate appetite and body weight.
  • Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments from approximately 40,000 users to investigate these accounts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that an experimental weight-loss drug that has not yet received regulatory approval is already attracting users willing to obtain unapproved versions online. Now, scientists are using artificial intelligence to investigate their experiences, uncovering unexpected symptom reports that differ from those documented in clinical trials.

Recent findings suggest that the drug, retatrutide, belongs to a upcoming generation of GLP-1 medications designed to help regulate appetite and body weight. Although it remains under investigation and is not approved for use, people are purchasing unapproved formulations that are not intended for human consumption and discussing their experiences on internet forums.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments from approximately 40,000 users to investigate these accounts. Their study, published in JAMA Network Open, provides the first systematic examination of potential side effects reported by people claiming to use unapproved retatrutide.

One finding stood out. Among owners whose reported symptoms could be classified, increased appetite was the most common complaint. That was particularly unexpected because retatrutide is designed to suppress hunger, and its Phase 2 clinical trials primarily identified digestive problems as the most frequent side effects.

AI Uncovers Unexpected Weight-Loss Drug Reports.

It has been revealed that "Our goal is to identify hypotheses in online conversations that we could test. AI helps us find recurring patterns in people's self-reports, including experiences that may be missed by conventional drug-safety monitoring," says Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS), Director of Penn's Computational Social Listening Lab and senior author of the study.

However, the researchers emphasize that the findings should not be interpreted as proof of previously unknown side effects. Reddit users represent a very different population from clinical trial participants, and their accounts cannot establish whether the drug caused the symptoms they described.

There is also considerable uncertainty about what these individuals are actually taking. Products sold outside regulated medical channels may differ from the genuine experimental medication in their ingredients, purity, and dosage.

"We can't say that retatrutide is causing these symptoms, or even that Reddit consumers are actually taking genuine retatrutide, since the drug is not legally available, and gray market formulations vary," says Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author of the study.

Rather than confirming newly introduced risks, the research offers scientists an opportunity to identify questions that warrant more rigorous investigation.

"This is the first glimpse into the experiences of a population that is otherwise outside conventional drug safety monitoring because they are taking unapproved versions of a drug that has yet to finish clinical trials," claims Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS.

How Researchers Analyzed 150,000 Reddit Posts.

Sources indicate that the project builds on previous research by the University of Pennsylvania team. In that earlier investigation, scientists used large language models (LLMs), the type of artificial intelligence that powers many modern chatbots, to examine more than 400,000 Reddit posts discussing semaglutide and tirzepatide.

That analysis revealed reports of possible side effects, including menstrual irregularities, that may not have been fully documented in clinical trials or official drug safety records.

"We wanted to apply the same methodology to gray-market retatrutide," says Sehgal.

Industry observers note that retatrutide is particularly interesting because it works differently from existing GLP-1 medications. Semaglutide acts on one hormone receptor involved in blood sugar control and appetite regulation, while tirzepatide targets two. Retatrutide activates three receptors, potentially producing a different combination of effects throughout the body.

According to recent reports, to investigate what people were experiencing, the researchers used AI to examine nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments. They identified approximately 14,000 users who claimed to have personally taken an unapproved version of retatrutide.

Sources indicate that the AI systems then extracted descriptions of symptoms that people associated with the medication and translated those descriptions into standardized medical terminology. This allowed researchers to compare reports even when different people used different words to describe similar experiences.

After excluding expected effects such as weight loss and reduced appetite, the team identified 7,823 customers who reported at least one symptom that could be medically classified.

"A researcher might be able to examine a few thousand Reddit posts by hand, but looking at nearly 150,000 would be an enormous undertaking," indicates Sehgal. "AI makes it possible to analyze these conversations at scale, identifying patterns in what people are sharing that would otherwise be difficult to recognize.".

A Surprising Appetite Paradox Emerges.

The most striking difference involved hunger.

According to recent reports, in retatrutide's Phase 2 clinical trials (the drug is presently in Phase 3 trials, the final step before FDA approval), participants most commonly experienced gastrointestinal complaints, including nausea. These effects are familiar concerns with medications that influence appetite and digestion.

But among Reddit users who reported taking unapproved retatrutide, the pattern looked different. Increased appetite emerged as the most frequently described classifiable symptom, despite the substantial weight-loss effects demonstrated in clinical testing.

The researchers also compared the upcoming findings with their earlier analysis of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

Compared with those earlier Reddit reports, discussions involving unapproved retatrutide contained proportionally more mentions of appetite-related changes, sleep disturbances, increased heart rate, and muscle-related symptoms. Reports of nausea and other digestive complaints were proportionally less common.

Industry observers note that these differences could reflect how retatrutide interacts with the body. However, they could also result from differences between the groups of people discussing the medications, their other drug use, or the contents of the unapproved products.

"Retatrutide works differently from existing GLP-1 drugs, so it's possible that its effects on the body are different, too," says Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study.

"But the people discussing it on Reddit also may be different," she notes. "Users willing to obtain an unapproved medication on the gray market likely differ from other clinical populations. Some may be taking multiple experimental peptides, and we can't verify exactly what they're taking. We need more research to understand what, if anything, these differences in self-reported symptoms mean.".

Can AI Detect Drug Safety Concerns Earlier?

Beyond the findings about retatrutide, the study demonstrates how AI could potentially improve the early detection of drug safety concerns.

In a recent development, traditional monitoring systems depend heavily on clinical trials, reports submitted to regulators, and information collected by healthcare professionals. People obtaining experimental medications through unapproved channels may not be represented in those systems.

Industry observers note that social media offers another source of information, allowing researchers to identify recurring experiences that might otherwise escape attention. However, these reports must be independently investigated before they can be considered reliable evidence of a drug-related problem.

The Penn team has already seen an example of how this approach can help guide further research.

Sources indicate that in their previous investigation of semaglutide and tirzepatide, researchers identified online reports of menstrual irregularities. Those findings subsequently encouraged another scientific team to examine similar symptoms using the FDA's database of reported adverse drug events.

Industry observers note that the follow-up study, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology, also detected disproportionate reports of certain menstrual changes. Although those findings did not establish causation, they provided additional reasons to investigate the potential connection.

The researchers hope their retatrutide findings will lead to similar independent studies, particularly as the drug advances through clinical development.

Industry observers note that "That's what we hope will happen with this study," claims Sehgal. "Other researchers can take what we find on Reddit and look for the same patterns in other datasets, using entirely different methods. Whether those signals hold up or not, the goal is to build a better understanding of what people are actually experiencing.".

The research was conducted through the University of Pennsylvania's School of Engineering and Applied Science and Perelman School of Medicine. Benjamin Rader of Boston Children's Hospital also contributed as a co-author. Funding was provided in part by the University of Pennsylvania's Penn Medical Communication Research Institute. Tronieri disclosed receiving an investigator-initiated grant from Novo Nordisk on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, along with consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. No conflicts of interest were reported by the other authors.

But the GPUs are out there, as hyperscalers, regional and AI-native cloud providers all quickly expand their capacity.

It has been revealed that how do we then connect AI compute capacity with the researchers who need it? How do we enable universities, national research labs and companies all over the world to build their own models?

This is what Hugging Face and NVIDIA are tackling with Training Cluster as a Service - providing GPU cluster accessibility, with the flexibility to only pay for the duration of training runs.

To get started, any of the 250,000 organizations on Hugging Face can request the GPU cluster size they need, when they need it.

To get started, you can request a GPU cluster on behalf of your organization at hf.co/training-cluster.

Training Cluster as a Service integrates key components from NVIDIA and Hugging Face into a complete solution:.

Once your GPU cluster request is accepted, Hugging Face and NVIDIA will collaborate to source, price, provision and set up your GPU cluster per your size, region and duration requirements.

The Telethon Institute of Genomics and Medicine - TIGEM for short - is a research center dedicated to understanding the molecular mechanisms behind rare genetic diseases and developing novel treatments. Training new AI models is a new path to predict the effect of pathogenic variants and for drug repositioning.

AI offers fresh ways to research the causes of rare genetic diseases and to develop treatments, but our domain requires training new models. Training Cluster as a Service made it easy to procure the GPU capacity we needed, at the right time.

-- Diego di Bernardo, Coordinator of the Genomic Medicine program at TIGEM.

Numina is a non-profit organization building open-source, open-dataset AI for reasoning in math - and won the 2024 AIMO progress prize.

We are tracking well on our objective to build open alternatives to the best closed-source models, such as Deepmind's AlphaProof. Computing resources is our bottleneck today - with Training Cluster as a Service we will be able to reach our goal!

-- Yann Fleureau, cofounder of Project Numina.

Mirror Physics is a startup creating frontier AI systems for chemistry and materials science.

Sources indicate that together with the MACE team, we're working to push the limits of AI for chemistry. With Training Cluster as a Service, we're producing high-fidelity chemical models at unprecedented scale. This is going to be a significant step forward for the field.

-- Sam Walton Norwood, CEO and founder at Mirror.

Training Cluster as a Service is a new collaboration between Hugging Face and NVIDIA to make AI compute more readily available to the global community of AI researchers.

In a recent development, access to large-scale, high-performance compute is essential for building the next generation of AI models across every domain and language. Training Cluster as a Service will remove barriers for researchers and companies, unlocking the ability to train the most advanced models and push the boundaries of what’s possible in AI.

-- Clément Delangue, cofounder and CEO of Hugging Face.

Sources indicate that integrating DGX Cloud Lepton with Hugging Face’s Training Cluster as a Service gives developers and researchers a seamless way to access high-performance NVIDIA GPUs across a broad network of cloud providers. This collaboration makes it easier for AI researchers and organizations to scale their AI training workloads while using familiar tools on Hugging Face.

-- Alexis Bjorlin, vice president of DGX Cloud at NVIDIA.

We are excited to collaborate with NVIDIA to offer Training Cluster as a Service to Hugging Face organizations - you can get started today at hf.co/training-cluster.

#172321. Has Rockstar taken the "Grand Theft Auto" out of GTA 6? Or has it just gamified car-jacking properly for the first time?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1270 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

Has Rockstar taken the "Grand Theft Auto" out of GTA 6? Or has it just gamified car-jacking properly for the first time?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's impossible to have a big game launch these days without some section of the internet, somewhere, finding grievances with the final product because it does not align with the expectations they had pre-release.
  • The most recent upset comes in the form of Grand Theft Auto 6's revised take on, well, grand theft auto.
  • It has been revealed that so it makes sense that the internet is in a bit of a spin about GTA 6's more mature and restrained take on its eponymous crime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's impossible to have a big game launch these days without some section of the internet, somewhere, finding grievances with the final product because it does not align with the expectations they had pre-release.

The most recent upset comes in the form of Grand Theft Auto 6's revised take on, well, grand theft auto. In case you're one of the few still unfamiliar, grand theft auto is more than the titular moniker for Rockstar's premier crime simulation series; it's actually a US legal term for the act of stealing or attempting to steal a motor vehicle. In most previous GTA entries, this was a central part of the core gameplay loop: accept a mission, nick a car, complete the mission, nick another car, getaway. It's an endemic part of the loop, and has become so popular and identifiable as such that even other games - Watch Dogs, Saint's Row, Cyberpunk 2077, and so on - have emulated the mechanic.

It has been revealed that so it makes sense that the internet is in a bit of a spin about GTA 6's more mature and restrained take on its eponymous crime. A quick, no-frills getaway in a vehicle you've hijacked on the road isn't always the most effective option. A mindless crime spree on the streets of Leonida is not a simple thing to pull off, nor an easy thing to live down. In this game, actions have consequences, and an ill-timed or ill-judged car jacking can rapidly and efficiently put an end to your criminal ambitions.

According to recent reports, that's not to say you cannot simply steal cars. Of course you can: the option to saunter up to an occupied vehicle and jack it from its registered owner is available to you from the very beginning of the game. But the citizens of Leonida aren't going to take your wanton act of foolishness lying down; many of the motorists in the county will fight back, pull a piece on you, or run you over mid-robbery attempt. Even if you are lucky to find one of the more pliant residents of the city, you might find something peculiar is happening in their car. I jacked a woman in the city over the weekend, and the cat she was ferrying from place to place decided to attack me, causing me to crash. I've heard other people say they've had muffled cries coming from the boot of the car where someone is transporting a hostage, or incidents where they've jacked the same person multiple times, leading to the poor car's owner to have a breakdown in the middle of the city.

According to recent reports, that cat event, the team here at Eurogamer has worked out, is an early game trigger - it seems stealing random cars early in the game will increase the chance of this encounter occurring. Rockstar's guiding hand is more visible here, then, in trying to teach you a lesson: don't steal cars. You're given your own - Jason's two-door coupé utility, a Vapid Creado - that I actually formed quite an emotional bond with in the opening 10-or-so hours of the game. 'Look after this car,' Rockstar insists, tutorialising you how to repair it, customise it, make it all pretty so it's in good condition when you go pick up Lucia for the first time.

Shortly after the 10 hour marker, narrative events whisk you away elsewhere and you're given a 'slim jim', a long, thin tool that allows you to break into locked cars - something you could only do with a quick elbow jab before. The benefit here is two-fold; you can break into cars without setting off their alarms, and without breaking glass and lowering their resale value (something quite notable in the earlier sections of the game). So, it takes you until Chapter 2 to start being able to more reliably and consistently break into vehicles. Good.

And it'll take even longer to break into keyless vehicles. We're in 2026 after all, and it's heavily implied this is when GTA 6 is also set - it stands to reason that many cars run keyless fobs, and your old-school tools won't cut it if you want to break into a Zorruso, rather than an old Vapid truck. But then, even when you're well-armed and ready to start an illustrious new career as Vice City's most nefarious car thief, there's more to consider. Most modern cars also come with trackers: standard trackers simply prevent you modding cars you don't own (not an matter you'll face very often), but advanced trackers are more problematic.

Recent findings suggest that boosting a car with an advanced tracker immediately alerts the cops to your location, and they close in on you fast. The only answer to this problem is flooring it, and outspeeding the signal ping the tracker is sending out: you need to drive fast and cleanly in order to stay mobile long enough for the tracker to deactivate, and this often incurs damage that makes selling these cars to fences a less viable option. You can't even sell cars with trackers installed at all to some fences until you're much, much further into the game.

It has been revealed that so, long story short, stealing cars is a faff in GTA 6. But I like that. I like that Rockstar has evolved the gameplay formula to more accurately reflect the state of the world in 2026. Modern problems require modern answers, and given that Rockstar has gone above and beyond in its creation of a sandbox simulation of Florida, I feel the immersion would be broken by just being able to saunter up to any car you want and break into it. No, needing a 'slim jim' or a key cloner - or needing to case my victims properly before trying to jack them - makes for a better game as far as I'm concerned. It makes me roleplay Jason and Lucia better, it makes me engage with the game's systems more, it makes me appreciate the cars that I do have whilst I have them.

It also improves the flow of the game and how I interact with missions. I recently played GTA: Vice City, and after most missions were wrapped up, I would simply fling the nearest motorist onto the sidewalk, hop in their car, and drive away into the Malibu-styled sunset. I can't simply do that in GTA 6: I need to think about my getaway options, whether there's heat on my car, and where my next best (and cheapest) ride is going to be if a robbery or raid goes awry. 'Ah,' I think, 'I understand why there's a garage next to that safehouse on the map now.'.

In making the act of grand theft auto harder and more awkward, Rockstar has nudged me into playing Grand Theft Auto the game like a more thoughtful criminal. I play it like someone on the run, who wouldn't just be indiscriminately committing wanton acts of felony theft on a whim, just because I didn't want to run four blocks down the road to meet my pals for a drink. It's a gorgeous example of functionality, design, and narrative dovetailing - one of the key reasons this is a five star game. The complaints about the system, to my ear, don't reflect what Rockstar has built here. Plus, if it bothers you that much, you could always try to play GTA 6 like a mindless thug if you really want to - just expect the world to treat you like one, too.

Nintendo raised the price of the Switch 2 earlier this year in response to rising NAND and DRAM prices, but on Black Friday, you can wipe out that hike with a variety of bundles available on Amazon. The core deal is the Mario Kart World Switch 2 bundle, which includes the game, the console, and three months of Nintendo Switch Online. Industry observers note that as you can read about in our Nintendo Switch 2 review published last year, the console is a major upgrade over the original version. The heart of the handheld is a custom Nvidia SoC that includes eight Arm Cortex-A78C CPU cores alongside an Nvidia GPU with 1,536 CUDA cores, hailing from the firm's Ampere generation. Sources indicate that showing off the capabilities of these upgraded internals is a larger 7.9-inch, 1080p LCD display. It's larger and brighter than the original Switch display, but it also comes with far greater capabilities, including variable refresh rate, HDR10 support, and a 120 Hz panel.

In a recent development, the handheld is much larger overall, and it sports a redesigned Joy-Con mechanism that's far more resilient than the original Switch design. The kickstand more closely aligns with the Switch OLED, running along most of the edge of the display; the original Switch props up the console on one side, where it can easily fall over.

Overall, the performance jump is what stands out most. Nintendo has released several Switch 2 updates for flagship titles like Metroid Prime 4 and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom with support for higher resolutions and frame rates. Titles like the recent Ocarina of Time Remake and Donkey Kong Bananza target 60 FPS, though occasionally fall short of that mark.

#172319. Tech Report: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 captures the franchise's bloody absurdity like nothing else

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1023 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 captures the franchise's bloody absurdity like nothing else

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that warhammer 40,000 is a universe of two distinct moods.
  • Perhaps the best praise I can give Boltgun 2 - which, like its 2023 predecessor, is developed by Auroch Digital - is that it honours 40k's sillier side wonderfully.
  • Recent findings suggest that like its predecessor, Boltgun 2 adopts the style of a retro first-person shooter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that warhammer 40,000 is a universe of two distinct moods. On the one hand, it's a grimdark future of serious, solemn stories where trillions die in galactic wars of attrition; of tragedies and insurmountable threats. But there's also the other side of Warhammer 40,000, where goofy hilarity and gory absurdity lies. Where Orks paint their cars go-faster red, and where chainaxe-wielding Khorne Berserkers indulge in gleeful hyperviolence.

Perhaps the best praise I can give Boltgun 2 - which, like its 2023 predecessor, is developed by Auroch Digital - is that it honours 40k's sillier side wonderfully. It's unashamedly gory, over-the-top, and, most crucially, fun. Its creators understand that after a long day at work, sometimes all you want to do is shred a guy or five.

Recent findings suggest that like its predecessor, Boltgun 2 adopts the style of a retro first-person shooter. It's a little bit Doom, a little bit Duke Nukem, as you blast through its low-poly environments and its sprite-based enemies, hoovering up - and using up - ammo and health as you go. I jumped in right as I was starting World of Warcraft: Forever. And in contrast to that game's slow burn beginning, Boltgun 2 is a full-throttle roar right from the word go that rarely lets up. Just moments in, you're belting down corridors - either playing as a Space Marine or a Sister of Battle, depending on your mood - and unloading endless rounds into cultists and Chaos dregs.

I should note that while I'm a Warhammer fan, the original Boltgun passed me by, so this sequel has been something of a revelation. It truly revels in its violent delights, indulging in its hunger for spectacle. As your bullets turn lesser goons into raspberry jam, strong animation work and excellent audio design bring its cartoonish brutality to life. And it's paired with some brilliantly over-the-top weaponry too. Take your basic Boltgun: when you pull the trigger, this beefed-up rifle's fist-sized projectiles erupt with a weighty bang. Weaker enemies get minced in their path, and for the Space Marine, this is the first gun.

Industry observers note that as a Space Marine, you've also got a devastating cool-down-based rush attack known as the Obliterating Charge. It's handy for repositioning in a pinch, but it also bursts through enemies with the power of a speeding lorry. The Space Marine has his chainsword for slice-and-dicing too, and tougher enemies really require some elbow grease - you really have to mash that melee button - to get through 'em. Is all this the height of video game sophistication? Absolutely not, but it got me grinning, and it's a visceral thrill that still hasn't lost its sheen.

I also love that the two selectable characters aren't just cosmetic swaps. If you opt for the Sister of Battle, she comes with her own distinct weapons and abilities. I adore her Flamer and the close-quarters havoc it can cause; the way fire roars from its nozzle as sparks fly and black smoke spews. And while she doesn't have an Obliterating Charge, she does get a slide move that's a fantastic way to maintain forward-momentum. Both characters have their own quirks and appeal - the Space Marine is slower and heavier, but offers punchier gunplay, while the Sister of Battle is swifter but lighter in combat - and both, I reckon, warrant their own playthroughs.

It'd also be remiss not to mention Boltgun 2's dedicated 'taunt' button. Both characters have their own voice lines and many are context-specific. It's a fun thing to spam mid-fight, or to hit when celebrating moments of especially grisly victory. I remembered hearing you could get some extra ammo or healing items if you threw a taunt at the floating servo skull that flies beside you throughout the game and, yup, it's true. Little details like that, alongside the smaller secrets hidden around each mission, create an FPS that's so far been a real joy to mess around in.

It's occasionally all a bit floaty, perhaps, but the combination of speed and action is a winner. What elevates it even further, though, are those Warhammer 40,000 flourishes. I've been amazed how swiftly levels introduce fresh enemies, and how lovingly they're depicted here. Basic Black Legion Chaos Space Marines take centre stage early on, but as you progress, new subfactions are introduced with their own unique quirks. Khorne-loving Berserkers thunder toward you at speed for painful melee strikes, while devilish Bloodletters lurch at your blind spots with giant swords in-hand. In a later mission things are flipped, and the melee-focused enemies are replaced by menacing ranged forces. Noise Marines carry giant sonic weapons that shoot from afar and disrupt your movement, all while their own daemon allies leap in.

There's also something to say about the variety of the missions you'll encounter. Often, you're given a choice of paths through the game, each with their own planets and battlegrounds. These can be snow-laden ruins, unruly jungles, or cities under siege, and things get even wilder the further you go into the game. And while it's not the sort of experience that encourages you to stand still, if you do you'll see some striking views.

There's a moment, not too far into Boltgun 2, when you find yourself in the bowels of a Khorne-controlled world. Here, literal rivers of blood flow, and you can't go two steps without someone or something rushing in. So I whip out a shotgun and charge on in, properly exhilarated by the chaos of it all as I blast stray enemies into mist. It takes a lot to stave off fatigue in a game with this sort of relentless action but Auroch manages it here.

Warhammer 40,000 is, I think, the sort of setting you can't do half-heartedly, and Boltgun 2 feels like a total embrace of the series' wilder, more absurd side. So far, around five hours in, it's a damn good FPS, retro or otherwise. You can grab it for just over £20, and it's even on sale as of writing. For that price it's a no-brainer.

#172318. Latest Update: MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells

📅 23 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1475 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1475 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water.
  • According to recent reports, the engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins.
  • Sources indicate that by directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.

According to recent reports, the engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a upcoming study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.

Sources indicate that by directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.

According to recent reports, in experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.

Industry observers note that "It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," indicates study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. ".

A Fresh Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle.

The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.

In a recent development, most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.

"Currently, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," notes Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's upcoming bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself.".

The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.

From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot.

The latest swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.

According to recent reports, for that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.

When illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.

The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.

Industry observers note that "People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman says. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny.".

It has been revealed that for the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.

They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.

In a recent development, the earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could swiftly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.

To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.

"For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman indicates. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells.".

Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot.

Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.

The researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.

This alignment was vital because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.

The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.

By adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.

According to recent reports, stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.

Sources indicate that the engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.

The team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.

How Light Makes the Living Robot Swim.

With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.

According to recent reports, the finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.

Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.

Sources indicate that "You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman states. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap.".

Recent findings suggest that to test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.

As the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.

Although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers now strategy to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a new approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.

According to recent reports, "Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman says. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments.".

The Office of Naval Research provided partial funding for this research.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA Isaac GR00T (Generalist Robot 00 Technology) is a research and development platform for building robot foundation models and data pipelines, designed to accelerate the creation of intelligent, adaptable robots.

In a recent development, today, we revealed the availability of Isaac GR00T N1.5, the first major revision to Isaac GR00T N1, the world’s first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills. This cross-embodiment model processes multimodal inputs, including language and images, to perform manipulation tasks across diverse environments. It is adaptable through post-training for specific embodiments, tasks, and environments.

In this blog, we’ll demonstrate how to post-train (fine-tune) GR00T N1.5 using teleoperation data from a single SO-101 robot arm.

Technical Blog for GR00T N1.5: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/gr00t-n1_5/.

Now accessible to developers working with a wide range of robot form factors, GR00T N1.5 can be easily fine-tuned and adapted using the affordable, open-source LeRobot SO-101 arm.

This flexibility is enabled by the EmbodimentTag system, which allows seamless customization of the model for different robotic platforms, empowering hobbyists, researchers, and engineers to tailor advanced humanoid reasoning and manipulation capabilities to their own hardware.

Before proceeding to installation, please check if you satisfy the prerequisites.

People can fine-tune GROOT N1.5 with any LeRobot dataset. For this tutorial, we will be using the table cleanup task as an example for fine-tuning.

Recent findings suggest that it's important to note that datasets for the SO-100 or SO-101 are not in GR00T N1.5's initial pre-training. As a result of this, we will be training it as a new_embodiment.

For this tutorial, you can either begin by creating your own custom dataset by following these instructions (recommended) or by downloading the so101-table-cleanup dataset from Hugging Face. The --local-dir argument specifies where the dataset will be saved on your machine.

In an on-premises Kubernetes environment, removing NAT can make the network simpler to inspect, reduce translation overhead, and let the data center route directly to workloads. But direct routing is not automatically the right choice.

The decision depends on what the organization controls and what it needs from the network. A team that owns the physical fabric, has enough address space, and is comfortable operating BGP may benefit from making pod networks directly routable. A smaller environment, a team without control of the underlay, or a cluster that benefits from network abstraction may be better served by NAT or an overlay.

Kubernetes is also changing the ground under these decisions: kube-proxy is set to drop IPVS support starting with version 1.43, with nftables as the replacement. For on-prem teams already reviewing their service data path, it is a good moment to ask whether NAT still belongs in it.

So the useful question is not how to eliminate NAT, but when the operational benefits of doing so justify the additional routing responsibility.

Sources indicate that NAT solves a real problem. It allows an internal network to use its own address space without requiring the surrounding infrastructure to know how to reach every endpoint inside it. This is especially useful when you don’t control the underlying network.

Sources indicate that however, an on-premises data center is different. When you control both the Kubernetes cluster and the surrounding physical network, you can make Kubernetes networks directly routable.

In our case, removing NAT had practical and architectural benefits. It improved network performance, reduced CPU load on the nodes, and removed the risk of conntrack tables filling up on Kubernetes hosts. A directly routed L3 model also works well for traffic balancing when a node has two uplinks.

According to recent reports, this does not mean eliminating NAT from the data center entirely. NAT can remain at the boundary of the on-premises network, for example on hardware firewalls. Inside the data center, however, Kubernetes networks can be directly routable, allowing the physical network to reach workloads using the same routing mechanisms it already uses elsewhere.

In a recent development, in our implementation, BGP connects the Kubernetes network to the data center fabric: BIRD runs on the nodes and advertises pod CIDRs and selected service addresses, while kube-router manages Kubernetes networking. We described this implementation in more detail in our earlier article on building a routable on-prem.

Kubernetes cluster with BGP and ECMP. The crucial point for this decision is not the particular stack, but the requirement it creates: the surrounding network must be able to accept and route Kubernetes prefixes safely. If the organization cannot or does not want to make the cluster part of its routing domain, keeping NAT or an overlay is usually the simpler choice.

Removing NAT alone does not make a network resilient. If every node still depends on one switch, one NIC, or one uplink, direct routing simply exposes the same physical single point of failure more clearly.

In a recent development, the resilience benefit appears when the physical topology supports multiple independent paths. In our setup, nodes connect to independent data center switches and ECMP can use equivalent routes across those paths. If one path disappears, traffic can continue over the other.

That distinction matters when deciding whether direct routing is worth the effort. Organizations with redundant uplinks and switches can integrate Kubernetes into an already resilient routed fabric. If the underlay itself has no path redundancy, removing NAT should not be presented as a high-availability improvement: the physical failure domain still dominates the design.

In a recent development, our stack is one example of how direct routing can be implemented, not a default recommendation for clusters that remove NAT. We chose kube-router because it supports a minimal installation as a binary and systemd service and covers the networking functions we need for this L3 design. BIRD handles route advertisements to the surrounding network.

In a recent development, other environments may reasonably choose Calico for conventional L3 routing or Cilium when an eBPF-based dataplane and its additional capabilities are useful. The choice of CNI and routing daemon is secondary to the architectural decision: first decide whether exposing Kubernetes prefixes to the physical network makes operational sense, then choose the implementation that fits the team’s requirements.

A directly routed Kubernetes network is not automatically better than an overlay or NAT-based architecture. Each model solves a different operational problem.

Sources indicate that NAT is a reasonable choice when the cluster needs to remain isolated from the surrounding address initiative, when pod addresses cannot be routed through the data center, or when the infrastructure team does not control the upstream network. It also keeps Kubernetes-specific prefixes out of the physical routing domain, which can be valuable for smaller environments where direct visibility into every pod is not important.

An overlay is useful when portability and abstraction matter more than exposing the physical packet path. It lets Kubernetes networking remain largely independent of the underlay and can simplify deployment across heterogeneous infrastructure. The tradeoff is another layer to inspect during troubleshooting and, depending on the implementation, encapsulation overhead.

Direct routing makes the most sense when the organization owns the physical network, has address space available for pod CIDRs, and has operators comfortable with BGP and route filtering. It becomes more attractive when preserving source addresses, using standard network troubleshooting tools, predictable performance, or integrating the cluster with redundant data center paths are key. At a larger scale, those operational benefits can justify the extra coordination between Kubernetes and network teams.

Sources indicate that the broader lesson is not that every Kubernetes cluster needs BGP or that NAT should disappear everywhere. It is that Kubernetes has matured enough that we should stop automatically treating its network as a black box.

According to recent reports, as more production and AI workloads move onto Kubernetes, network architecture becomes part of application reliability. In an on-premises data center, BGP and ECMP give us the option to use the resilience already available in the physical network rather than building another isolated networking layer on top of it.

It has been revealed that sometimes the best way to make Kubernetes networking more robust is not to add another abstraction, but to remove one. But only when the surrounding infrastructure and the team operating it are ready to take responsibility for the routing that abstraction previously hid.

If most of those answers are yes, direct routing is worth serious consideration. If not, NAT or an overlay may be the more resilient operational choice—not because it is technically more advanced, but because it better matches the environment.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.

In a recent development, researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a newly introduced type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.

Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.

It has been revealed that the researchers believe their latest design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.

A Newly introduced Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision.

Recent findings suggest that traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.

Recent findings suggest that to accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.

"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system.".

The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.

Another crucial advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.

A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare.

Sources indicate that to evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.

Recent findings suggest that when used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.

It has been revealed that the healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.

It has been revealed that the researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.

"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," remarked Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment.".

The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.

Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough.

Sources indicate that the fresh spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.

Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.

The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.

"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible.".

Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.

Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices.

The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.

It has been revealed that in industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is presently practical.

Recent findings suggest that healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.

Recent findings suggest that "Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work highlights that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day.".

According to recent reports, as photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a latest generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that one of the first rules I learned when I entered the job market was: never work for free. Adam Driver and Steven Soderbergh didn't care much about that rule, because they had been given such strong assurances that Disney would approve their Star Wars film, The Hunt for Ben Solo.

In a upcoming interview with Sam Fragoso on the “Talk Easy” podcast, Driver (who played Ben Solo/Kylo Ren in the Star Wars sequel trilogy from 2015 to 2019​​​​​​​) told Fragoso​​​​​​​ that then-Lucasfilm president Kathleen Kennedy had reassured both Driver and Soderbergh that the movie would happen, and that Disney was on board.

With that validation in mind, Driver and Soderbergh continued to work on The Hunt for Ben Solo for free, until the project was canceled.

“We were gonna do a Ben Solo movie and that didn’t happen," Driver told Fragoso​​​​​​​. "And we worked on it for a long time. Soderbergh did that for nothing, because we were given a lot of confidence. Like Kathy [Kennedy] said, we have​​​​​​​ a 100% approval rate [from Disney]. We worked on it. No one’s paying us to work on it. The only reason we were working on it was we fucking loved the idea, how we wanted to do it, and I loved that character.”.

Driver stated their love for the project and the character was their “guiding principle,” and that they were even figuring out how to make it on a low budget so they could realize their vision for the movie.

Because Kennedy was confident Disney would approve the project, Driver and Soderbergh believed the money would come later, once it was greenlit.

Industry observers note that that turned out not to be the case. Kennedy, vice president Cary Beck, and former chief creative officer (and current Lucasfilm co-president) Dave Filoni were interested, but Disney studio executives Bob Iger and Alan Bergman shut the project down. Their reason? They couldn’t see how Ben Solo could still be alive. That’s a bit rich coming from a franchise where Darth Vader and Anakin Skywalker haunt the narrative around the clock — but we digress.

Earlier this month, Driver also confirmed on The Rich Eisen Show that his character wouldn't be returning and that the dream was over. “No more Star Wars,” Driver noted. “We tried to do one more, but they’re like, ‘No, he’s dead.’”.

According to recent reports, it’s a sad ending for a character people clearly wanted to see more of. But the worst part isn’t that we’ll never see the project come to fruition; it’s that Driver and Soderbergh weren’t paid a dime for it. Never work for free, folks.

In a recent development, windows 7 may have been retired years ago, but that hasn’t stopped enthusiasts from finding ways to bring modern hardware and features to Microsoft’s beloved operating system. A newly introduced community project is now giving Windows 7 the ability to support modern Nvidia, AMD, and Intel graphics cards, along with DirectX 12 and Vulkan 1.4 capabilities.

According to recent reports, developed by enthusiasts EAZY BLACK, kryptik, and VisualEhrmanntraut, the project backports WDDM 2.2 from Windows 10. Interestingly, Windows 7 originally released with WDDM 1.1, while Microsoft introduced WDDM 2.0 with Windows 10 in 2015 and WDDM 2.2 with the Creators Upgrade in 2017. Microsoft also introduced a limited version of DirectX 12 for Windows 7 in 2019; however, that implementation was only meant for developers to port select games to the older operating system.

According to a post by @TheBobPony on X, Nvidia's RTX 40 and RTX 50 series, AMD's Radeon RX 7000 and RX 9000 series, and select Intel Arc graphics cards are supported. Screenshots confirm that the backport enables GPUs to be recognized by Windows 7 as well as third-party apps like GPU-Z. It is also claimed that features such as ray tracing and DLSS also work on compatible hardware. Older GPUs, including Nvidia's RTX 30 series and AMD's Radeon RX 6000 series, may also benefit from the project. That mentioned, actual feature support depends on the graphics card, driver implementation, and application.

According to recent reports, for anyone who still prefers Windows 7 or relies on older software and hardware, this project is worth exploring, especially if you intend to extend the usefulness of the operating system. Customers can also combine it with the VxKex compatibility layer, allowing newer Windows apps to run on older operating systems. You can grab the project files and modified drivers by heading to the W7Revived website.

There’s a reason why enthusiasts continue to keep Windows 7 alive. Released in 2009 as a successor to Windows Vista, it offered a familiar interface, solid performance, and a straightforward desktop experience. It became one of Microsoft’s most popular operating systems and remained a favorite among PC enthusiasts and everyday users long after the arrival of Windows 10.

It has been revealed that in fact, Windows 7 still has some life left in it. We recently tested the aging operating system against Windows 11 on a modern PC running on an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, Radeon RX 6950 XT, and 64GB of DDR5 memory. The tests included eight DirectX 11 and two DirectX 9 titles, with Windows 7 delivering better performance in certain scenarios, particularly CPU-bound games, along with stronger 1% lows in some titles.
