Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

In a recent development, "Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages. Most AI apps send both to the same large model and pay large-model prices for each one.

Model routing fixes that. A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.

In this guide we'll cover what model routing is, how routers decide, and what it saves. Then we'll build a small router in about 60 lines of JavaScript and run it over 200 customer messages. At one setting it matched a large model's accuracy for about a third of the cost. At another it came within a point and a half for 89% less.

Model routing in AI is the practice of sending each request to the model best suited to it, instead of sending every request to one model. A router sits between your app and a pool of models, reads each request, and picks a model based on what you care about: cost, speed, or quality.

In a recent development, you'll also see it called AI model routing, LLM routing, or LLM model routing. They all mean the same thing. The pool might be a small and a large model from one provider, or models from several providers behind one API.

According to recent reports, the idea rests on one observation: most requests are easy. A small model answers them as well as a large one, in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the price. The router's whole job is finding the hard ones.

The diagram below highlights a typical AI model routing architecture.

In a recent development, model routing works in three steps: the router reads the request, decides which model should answer it, and forwards the request to that model. The middle step is where routers differ. Routing tools decide which model to use in one of four ways.

Sources indicate that rule-based routing uses rules you write by hand. Requests from free-initiative consumers go to a small model. Anything tagged as code goes to a coding model. Prompts over a certain length go to a model with a bigger context window. It's simple, predictable, and free to run, but the rules only know what you thought of in advance.

Industry observers note that intelligent model routing uses a model to make the decision. A small, fast classifier reads each request and predicts which model in the pool will answer it well. You'll also see it called smart or dynamic model routing.

In a recent development, two more terms come up here. Task-aware routing picks a model by the kind of job, like summarising, coding, or answering a support question. Context-aware routing also looks at what surrounds the request, like the conversation so far, the user, or the tools available.

Industry observers note that the major platforms work this way. Microsoft describes its Foundry model router as "a trained language model" that picks a model for each prompt in real time. Google says Gemini Notebook uses its new Decisions API as a real-time router, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. I've tested the Google Decisions API against Jev on the same messages we'll use below.

Cascade routing tries the cheapest model first and only moves up when the answer isn't good enough. The usual test is confidence: if the cheap model is sure, keep its answer. If it isn't, send the request to a stronger model. It's also called confidence-based routing, and it's what we'll build below.

A cascade needs no separate classifier, because the first model's own confidence does the routing. The trade-off is that escalated requests pay for two models and wait for both.

Fallback routing is about staying up, not saving money. If a model times out, hits a rate limit, or its provider has an outage, the router sends the request to the next model on a list. Most production routers combine fallbacks with one of the three methods above.

The main benefits of model routing in AI systems are lower cost, faster responses, and fewer outages, without giving up quality on the hard requests.

Industry observers note that we'll build a cascade router for a job every support tool has: sorting customer messages. Each message gets one of ten labels, like atm support or request refund.

Industry observers note that the test set is 200 messages from Banking77, a public set of banking support messages: ten labels, 20 messages each. They're the same 200 messages from my zero shot classification test, which is where the single-model numbers below come from.

Recent findings suggest that put both keys in a .env file and run the examples with node --env-file=.env. It's the same setup as in my guide to getting a YouTube API key.

Sources indicate that create router.mjs. The first function sends the message to Jev with one multiple-choice question, and returns the label Jev picked along with its confidence:.

Confidence runs from 0 to 1. When nearly all the probability sits on one label, it's close to 1. When Jev is torn between two labels, it drops.

Sources indicate that the second function asks Claude Opus 5.5 the same question. The output_config block limits the answer to one of our labels, so there's no free text to parse. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema explains how that works.

The router itself is about a dozen lines:.

If Jev is at least 80% confident, its answer goes straight back. If not, Claude answers instead. And if Claude fails, the router falls back to Jev's answer, because a shaky answer beats an error page.

Try it on an easy message and a harder one:.

Jev was sure about the lost card. On the ATM question it leaned towards card acceptance with a confidence of 0.64, so the router asked Claude, which got it right.

Because cheap, strong, and threshold are options, the same function routes between any two models.

According to recent reports, model routing reduces AI costs by keeping easy requests on a cheap model and paying for the expensive one only when it's needed. Here's what that looked like on our 200 messages, starting with each model on its own:.

Opus gets six more messages right out of 200, and costs more than 120 times as much.

Now the router, at four confidence thresholds:.

Sources indicate that speed improved too. At the 0.8 threshold, the messages Jev kept came back in a median of 227 ms. The ones that escalated took about 2.1 seconds, because they waited for both models.

Recent findings suggest that A note on method: I ran every message through both models once and saved the answers, then replayed the router over them at each threshold. That's how you compare thresholds without paying for the same test four times.

Recent findings suggest that then I ran the router live to check. At 0.95 it scored the same 95.0% and sent 61 messages to Opus. At 0.8 it scored 93.5% and sent 20, a point under the replay. Two answers moved: one of Jev's confidence scores landed at 0.82 instead of 0.78, just over the line, and Opus changed its answer on one message. Scores near the threshold shift a little between runs, so leave yourself a margin.

The choice of cheap model matters less than you'd think. With Google's Gemini Decision 1 in first place instead of Jev, a 0.7 threshold reached the same 95% for US$0.28 per 1,000 messages.

It has been revealed that model routing can cost a little quality, and the threshold decides how much. In our test the gap to Opus ranged from nothing at 0.95 to two points at 0.7.

The loss comes from one place: answers the cheap model got wrong while feeling sure. At the 0.8 threshold, Jev kept five wrong answers because its confidence was above the line. Opus got four of those five wrong as well, so only one was a real loss: "Do all ATMs take this card?", which Jev filed under card acceptance with a confidence of 0.91.

Escalating isn't risk-free either. On one message, Jev had the right label with a confidence of 0.44, and Opus overruled it with the wrong one.

It has been revealed that to optimize costs using AI model routing, measure first, route second, and keep measuring. These six steps cover LLM model routing cost optimization for any pair of models:.

The return is easy to estimate once you know the split. If nine in ten requests stay on a model that costs 1% as much, the bill drops by about 89%, which is what we measured.

It has been revealed that several inference providers have multi-model routing built in, and most AI gateway platforms support model routing too, so you don't have to write your own. As of November 2026, these are the top model routing solutions for AI apps. Each name links to the tool's model routing docs:.

Industry observers note that hosted model routing platforms for large language models decide for you, which is the fastest way to start. A hand-built router like ours takes more work, but you choose the signal and you can see why every request went where it did.

It has been revealed that an LLM router is the component that does model routing for large language models. It can be a function in your own code, like the one in this guide, a hosted model such as Microsoft Foundry's model router, or a feature of an AI gateway.

Sources indicate that smart model routing is another name for intelligent model routing: a model, not a hand-written rule, decides where each request goes. Dynamic model routing means the same thing.

The ROI of AI model routing depends on how much of your traffic a cheaper model can handle. In our test, a 0.8 threshold kept 89.5% of messages on the cheap model and cut the cost per 1,000 messages from US$1.96 to US$0.22, for about a point of accuracy. The build was about 60 lines of code.

Sources indicate that openRouter's auto model routing works through its Auto Router. You set the model to openrouter/auto, and a decision model picks a model and a reasoning effort for each request. You pay the standard rate of whichever model it selects, with no extra fee.

It has been revealed that openClaw model routing is a primary model plus an ordered list of fallbacks. In the OpenClaw model routing configuration you set agents.defaults.model.primary and agents.defaults.model.fallbacks, and an agent can override the fallback list. When a model fails, OpenClaw first rotates auth profiles on the same provider, then moves to the next model on the list, as its model failover docs describe. That makes it fallback routing, not cost-based routing.

An AI gateway simplifies model routing by putting every model behind one API, one set of keys, and one place for logs. Your app calls the gateway, and the routing rules live in config instead of code, so changing a model doesn't need a deploy.

According to recent reports, mid-stream failover is when a router switches models after a streamed response has already started, because the first model failed partway through. It's the hardest kind of failover, because the user has already seen part of an answer. Many routers only fail over before the first token arrives and return an error after that, so check what your gateway does.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rob Versaw, Product Strategy at Dynatrace, bridging innovation and business impact.

​Headcount is an easy lever to pull—and often the wrong one. Before approving the next hire or the next AI license, look at where the work is actually waiting.

“We’re growing our engineering department. Why is it taking longer to get a product to market?”.

I’ve heard some version of that question from founders, CEOs and boards in medical devices, industrial tech and software. The budget goes up, the org chart grows, and release dates still slip.

In a recent development, the instinct to hire through a delivery problem is old, and so is the evidence against it. Computer scientist Fred Brooks, drawing on IBM’s OS/360 program, concluded that “adding manpower to a late software project makes it later.” Upcoming people need to learn the product and the organization. Experienced contributors spend time bringing them up to speed. Communication grows, and some work just can’t be split across more people. The same problem demonstrates up outside software when work is tightly connected and integration is hard.

The first question isn’t asking how many more people you need. It’s asking where the work’s getting stuck. AI makes that question more important, not less.

In a recent development, my own path ran from software engineering and information security in defense aerospace, through product and engineering leadership at industrial manufacturers and a dental implant maker, to a health tech startup. I saw the same thing more than once: A structure that worked with 15 engineers didn’t work with 40, but the organization had grown without redesigning how decisions were made.

Jim Collins described getting the right people in the right seats in Good to Great. The catch is that the seats change as the company grows. A capable engineer is promoted into management without the interest, skills or support to lead. A technical lead still reviews everyone’s work personally. Upcoming developers add coding capacity, while testing remains the bottleneck.

The promotion problem is measurable. Researchers at Yale, MIT and the University of Minnesota conducted a study of more than 200 firms and found that firms promoted top performers into management roles they weren’t well-suited for. Among those promoted, prior individual performance was negatively correlated with managerial quality. Management isn’t the next stage of engineering. It’s a different job.

Sources indicate that as teams grow, management often adds reviews and sign-offs to keep track of the work. Each one looks reasonable on its own. Together, they create waiting time. If approvals are covering for unclear ownership or missing capability, another gate rarely fixes that. It just makes the queue longer.

It has been revealed that at one dental technology software business, the delivery problem wasn’t a shortage of developers. Verification sat at the end of the line; defects surfaced late, and a fix sent work back through the queue. Each market or customer variant was effectively its own build, which multiplied the verification effort every time we released.

We changed two things. First, we shifted testing left. Test engineers joined design reviews, acceptance criteria were written alongside requirements, and automated verification ran with every change. Second, we moved to build once, configure many: a single validated core with market and customer differences handled through controlled configuration rather than separate code branches. Verification stopped growing with every new variant, and design-control evidence got simpler to produce.

In a recent development, we didn’t fix that by hiring. We changed how the work moved and who owned the decisions.

According to recent reports, 1. Review roles before approving more hires. Where is work waiting, what capability is actually missing, and who owns the result? Another developer adds little if completed work is already sitting in a verification queue.

2. Match responsibilities to capabilities and interests. Give strong engineers a technical career path that doesn’t require managing people. Support newly introduced managers with training, mentoring and clear expectations from the start.

3. Keep one visible set of priorities. When urgent manufacturing or customer work arrives, decide explicitly what moves. I once worked with a firm running 19 active projects with 14 design engineers. We didn’t need a fancier planning system. We needed fewer things competing for the same people.

Sources indicate that AI coding tools can make a developer faster without speeding up delivery overall. DORA’s 2026 analysis of AI in software development described exactly this tension: AI speeds up initial code generation, but some of the time saved goes into checking the output. It also linked higher AI adoption with both higher delivery throughput and higher delivery instability.

That matters because the bottleneck doesn’t disappear; it moves. If developers generate more code while testing, review, integration and decision rights stay the same, more work piles up at the same choke points. A team can feel flat out without getting much more product into customers’ hands.

Buying AI licenses can become another way of hiring through the problem. The tool may well be useful, but if the system around it is slow, more output at the front end will expose that weakness, not fix it.

The TGA requires device manufacturers to run a quality management system for the design, production, packaging, labeling and final inspection of a device, referencing ISO 13485:2016. Design controls define what evidence must exist and who is accountable. They don’t require a senior leader to approve every drawing. Clear roles can make compliance easier because ownership is visible when the auditor asks.

The same problem applies whether it’s an ASX 200 software company or a 30-person startup. More people, or more AI-generated output, won’t make up for unclear ownership, competing priorities and slow decisions.

According to recent reports, before adding people, tools or another approval step, find where the work is stuck. The answer may be a different assignment, a missing skill, fewer priorities or a decision that management needs to let someone else make.

Then ask the harder question: Will the structure that works today still work at next year’s scale?

Upskill your LLMs With Gradio MCP Servers Have you ever wanted your favorite Large Language Model (LLM) to do more than just answer questions? What if it could edit images for you, browse the web, or organize your email inbox?

Sources indicate that well, now it can! In this blog post, I'll show you:.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables developers to build secure, two-way connections between an LLM and a set of tools. For example, if you create an MCP server that exposes a tool capable of transcribing a video, then you can connect an LLM client (such as Cursor, Claude Code, or Cline) to the server. The LLM will then know how to transcribe videos and use this tool for you depending on your request.

In short, an MCP server is a standard way to upskill your LLM by granting it a new ability. Think of it like the apps on your smartphone. On its own, your smartphone can't edit images, but you can download an app to do this from the app store. Now, if only there were an app store for MCP servers? 🤔.

Hugging Face Spaces is the world's largest collection of AI applications. Most of these spaces perform a specialized task with an AI model. For example:.

Industry observers note that these spaces are implemented with Gradio, an open source python package for creating AI-powered web servers. As of version 5.28.0, Gradio apps support the MCP protocol.

That means that Hugging Face Spaces is the one place where you can find thousands of AI-powered abilities for your LLM, aka the MCP App Store!

It has been revealed that want to browse the app store? Visit this link. Manually, you can filter for MCP Compatible in https://hf.co/spaces.

Flux.1 Kontext[dev] is an impressive model that can edit an image from a plain text prompt. For example, if you ask it to "dye my hair blue" and upload a photo of yourself, the model will return the photo but with you having blue hair!

It has been revealed that let's plug this model as an MCP server into an LLM and have it edit images for us. Follow these steps:.

Using a popular public space as a tool may mean you have to wait longer to receive results. If you visit the space, you can click "Duplicate This Space" to create a private version of the space for yourself. If the space is using "ZeroGPU", you may need to revision to a PRO account to duplicate it.

This blog post has walked you through the exciting newly introduced capabilities that the Model Context Protocol (MCP) brings to Large Language Models. We've seen how Gradio apps, particularly those hosted on Hugging Face Spaces, are now fully MCP compliant, effectively turning Spaces into a vibrant "App Store" for LLM tools. By connecting these specialized MCP servers, your LLM can transcend basic question-answering and gain powerful new abilities, from image editing to transcription, to anything you can imagine!

Samsung Odyssey G8 G80SH 32-inch 4K OLED gaming monitor review: Color, performance and style

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2285 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Samsung Odyssey G8 G80SH is one of the best HDR OLEDs I’ve reviewed.
  • In a recent development, why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you’re shopping for one of the best OLED gaming monitors, the 240 Hz QHD category offers the most choices and the best bang for the buck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Samsung Odyssey G8 G80SH is one of the best HDR OLEDs I’ve reviewed. It delivers a stunning image with no need for calibration and addictive gaming that will keep you playing for hours.

Dynamic tone mapping for HDR10 content.

Matte anti-glare screen is very effective.

In a recent development, why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re shopping for one of the best OLED gaming monitors, the 240 Hz QHD category offers the most choices and the best bang for the buck. But 4K at 240 Hz is creeping downward in price and only represents a small upcharge. It also means that you can go to 32 inches and maintain good pixel density. If you have enough video card horsepower to push frame rates over 180fps, the quality is unmatched.

Samsung slides into the neither-expensive-nor-inexpensive position with its Odyssey G8 G80SH. This 32-inch Quantum Dot OLED runs 240 Hz at 4K resolution with Adaptive-Sync, HDR10, HDR10+, wide gamut color, factory calibration, and high brightness for HDR content. Let’s take a look.

Quantum Dot Organic Light Emitting Diode.

Max Resolution and Refresh Rate.

According to recent reports, first, I want to clear up any potential confusion with another recently reviewed Samsung display, the G80HS. That is a 6K resolution dual-refresh mode model that currently costs around $1,600. The G80SH I’m covering here is a 4K screen with a single 240 Hz mode, and it’s currently selling for $900.

Industry observers note that the G80SH delivers the best of everything in the premium OLED category. It’s 4K with a Quantum Dot layer that delivers a measured 106% coverage of DCI-P3. That’s about average among the QD-OLEDs I’ve tested, which range from 104 to 108%. The visual difference there is extremely small, not enough to affect a purchase decision. The G80SH also offers excellent out-of-the-box accuracy courtesy of a factory calibration. Though my sample didn’t need any tweaking, it benefited from a few adjustments. And that capability extends to HDR content, where you have full control of color temp, brightness, and luminance tracking.

Speaking of HDR, you get the requisite HDR10 support that all monitors have, plus Samsung’s answer to Dolby Vision, HDR10+. This extension of HDR10 includes dynamic tone mapping where the content matches its luminance curve to whatever display it’s shown on. Since HDR is mastered to a specific peak luminance, usually 1,000 nits but sometimes as high as 10,000, it’s beneficial when the screen can adapt to the incoming metadata to accommodate a lower or higher limit. You’ll see the same fine detail and nuance that the content creator did.

It has been revealed that gaming benefits from the aforementioned 240 Hz refresh rate plus a flawless implementation of Adaptive-Sync. The G80SH works with equal precision on G-Sync and FreeSync platforms, as well as the VRR output from gaming consoles. To help with your aim, there are reticles available in different colors and shapes, with a dynamic mode that keeps them in contrast with the background.

Like every Samsung monitor I’ve experienced, the G80SH delivers high style and solid build quality. The main color is silver, which you can see everywhere except the front, keeping the screen and surrounding bezel all black. There’s a matte anti-glare coating too, effectively eliminating all ambient light reflections. If you have a sunny room, this monitor can handle it without a degradation in image quality. You also get the latest video interfaces, four in total, plus USB and a headphone jack. LED lighting is featured on the back and can be controlled from the OSD.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

It has been revealed that so, just to recap before we jump into the tests, this is the Odyssey G8 G80SH, a 4K 240 Hz OLED that sells for $900. If you’re interested in learning more about the 6K model, my review from a few months ago is here.

According to recent reports, samsung still uses crumbly foam to ship its monitors, and my G80SH sample arrived safe and sound. The base, upright, and stand assemble with a captive bolt and a snap-on to create a solid package. To keep the panel thin, the power supply is external. It’s quite large, so consider that when fitting it into your space. The accessory bundle includes right-angle power cables plus one each of DisplayPort, HDMI, and USB-C.

In a recent development, the G80SH’s silver trim is visible from the front in the base and a thin border around the screen that wraps around from the back. The actual bezel is very narrow and flush, so you can’t see it when the power’s off. A small protrusion in the bottom center notes Samsung in tiny letters and houses an equally tiny power LED that can’t be seen from the front. Samsung is one of the few manufacturers to offer matte-screened OLEDs, and this implementation is excellent. Even a bright flashlight can’t throw a reflection onto the screen. Sunny office dwellers, this is your monitor.

In the back, it’s all silver all the time with a smooth finish and minimalist styling. There’s a thin ventilation grill on top, a small logo on one side, and hooray, inputs that face backward. You get two HDMI 2.1, a DisplayPort 2.1, USB-C with 98 watts, and two USB-A downstream ports. There are no internal speakers, but there is a 3.5mm headphone jack. On one side of the I/O panel is a joystick, the G80SH’s sole control key. Around the stand’s attachment point is an LED ring with colors and effects available in the OSD. If you remove the stand, a 100mm VESA mount is revealed should you prefer an aftermarket solution. Fasteners are not included.

According to recent reports, that large external power supply keeps the panel thin at just under two inches. The stand is solid and wobble-free and offers 2/25 degrees tilt, 30 degrees swivel, a 90-degree portrait mode and a 4.7-inch height range. Movements are firm and smooth, in keeping with the G80SH’s premium status.

It has been revealed that the G80SH’s OSD keeps Samsung’s traditional gaming monitor styling with its control panel appearance. Up top are portholes that deliver information about game-related settings. No refresh rate info, though. It would be nice to have that.

Recent findings suggest that in the Game menu, you get an Adaptive-Sync toggle, aiming points, a black equalizer to enhance shadow detail, and the LED lighting control. The reticles come in two shapes and three colors. Or you can use AI Mode, which changes the color to maintain contrast with the background. You can also position the aiming point somewhere other than the center of the screen. The lighting has multiple effects or can remain a single static color. One miss here is a frame counter. There’s no way to monitor the refresh rate.

In the Picture menu are all the G80SH’s calibration controls. You get five color temps, all adjustable, and seven gamma presets. The Contrast Enhancer is a field dimming control. True variable brightness is only active in HDR mode. You can choose between static and active tone mapping for HDR, which is handy for HDR10 content because it helps bring out highlights without clipping fine shadow detail.

You won’t find an sRGB mode among the color space choices, but if you pick Auto, the G80SH will render sRGB for SDR content. This is an approach that I like, and almost no other manufacturers do it that way. If you’d rather see the full gamut for all content, just leave it on Native. Peak Brightness does just what it says for HDR content; it raises the peak output. In my HDR tests, I saw 530 nits from a 25% window pattern.

Remaining menu items include port version control, an off timer, DSC toggle, and USB-C control. You also get two panel care options: logo brightness (dimming, actually) and pixel refresh. You can pause the incoming video signal while this is running if you wish.

In a recent development, the G80SH includes a factory calibration with a report saved in the monitor’s firmware. I found visually perfect color and grayscale tracking, but gamma was a little light. Two clicks of the gamma slider made that much better. I noted that though the default picture mode is called Eco, it is just as bright as the other presets, so that you can use it for all content. In HDR mode, you get Display HDR, which has excellent tone mapping and color accuracy. Suppose you want sRGB; just set Color Space to Auto. Then the G80SH will automatically render sRGB for SDR and the full gamut for HDR, which covers 106% of DCI-P3. If you want full color for SDR, set it to Native. My recommended settings are below.

The G80SH’s color quality and accuracy make it well suited for duty as a post-production monitor or perhaps an on-site display for location shoots. Only a slight gamma anomaly separates it from perfection. It nails grayscale and gamut tracking, which you can read about on pages four and five. And it’s bright enough for any indoor space. I noted that there was no variable brightness option for SDR, but you can turn on a dynamic contrast option, which equates to field dimming. In HDR mode, dimming occurs at the pixel level, and you can choose between Active and Static tone mapping. The former delivers more punch to HDR10 content.

I also noted the G80SH’s excellent color balance. SDR lets you choose between Native and Auto. Native shows the full gamut, which covers 106% of DCI-P3 and is very colorful. It will be the likely choice for most users. If you prefer sRGB for SDR, set the color space to Auto. Then, it will switch automatically. This is something very few monitors offer. I also noted that the HDR mode allows calibration of grayscale and gamma, another thing I rarely see.

Recent findings suggest that with the image dialed in, I turned to a few afternoons of gaming where the G80SH provided the addictive quality that all premium OLEDs have. It doesn’t have a frame counter, so I had to use FRAPS to monitor the refresh rate, which stayed around 200fps at the max detail settings in Doom Eternal. This was fast enough to provide blur-free motion and input lag low enough to keep up with my most frenetic movements. You’ll see on the next page that it offers response typical of other 4K 240 Hz OLEDs. That means you’ll be able to aim and shoot with speed and precision. I got extra credit in hoard mode for jump shots where I was able to land grenades on target while flying through the air. Turn and shoot became second nature as I mowed through my opponents.

In a recent development, detail in close encounters made me stop and admire the picture more than a few times. Tiny highlights like sweat and other bodily fluids popped right out, making the characters look three-dimensional. Other textures like stone and metal looked better thanks to strong reflections. These highlights moved smoothly over objects like the player’s weapon, which further enhanced realism. The G80SH has some of the best-looking HDR I’ve seen of late.

It has been revealed that it makes a great workday monitor too, with understated styling that stands out but doesn’t scream for attention. The LED lighting is just a ring in the back with smoothly playing effects or static colors available, or you can shut it off. The stand is rock solid with comfortable and usable ergonomics. The joystick navigates the OSD intuitively and efficiently. I really appreciated the rear-facing ports, which were easy to see and access. You get two USB-A downstream ports, which can accommodate peripherals once you make a connection to the USB-C input, which doubles as a charger with 98 watts of power. There are no internal speakers, but headphones plug into the 3.5mm jack.

Recent findings suggest that takeaway: If Samsung keeps the G80SH’s price below $1,000, it will sell a lot of them. It’s a super versatile display for any form of productivity or entertainment. It’s addictive for gaming, with smooth operation and quick response. The image looks stunning in every respect, whether moving or static. Color accuracy is good enough that calibration isn’t required. It has unique but understated styling and excellent ergonomics with a solid stand and rear-facing ports. Aside from a lack of internal speakers, there is nothing missing here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A near-record share of young adults won’t be traveling home to visit family for the holidays—they’re already living there. One in three U.S. adults between age 18 and 34 live with their parents, according to a new report from Realtor.com. That’s 25.2 million or 33% of young adults living at home in 2025, only a sliver less than the 33.6% during the pandemic-era peak in 2020. Living at home is one way that Americans who can’t afford to buy or rent on their own wrestle with the high cost of housing and other expenses. While the cost of housing is a nationwide problem, the share of adults living with their parents offers an interesting glimpse into regional affordability patterns around the country. “The pattern of young adults at home has spread beyond the most expensive markets, with the share rising most in parts of the South and West, including some that have traditionally supported an earlier launch,” Realtor.com’s chief economist, Danielle Hale, wrote in the report. “As young people adapt to high housing costs, they are delaying homeownership and the wealth creation that comes with it.” Two stories with the same ending Predictably, at least one of the country’s priciest cities is among those with the largest share of adults living with their parents—but the full story is more complicated. New York leads the list, with 41.3% of adults between the ages of 18 and 24 staying in the nest. In Philadelphia, Miami, Baltimore, and Houston, more than 38% of adults in that age range lived with their parents. Across Los Angeles, Atlanta, and Chicago, the share of adults living at home was over 35%. Houston, Atlanta, and Baltimore aren’t known for their high cost of living, unlike costly urban hubs like New York and Los Angeles, but home prices have soared in recent years in those markets. That rapid change to local affordability is freezing many young adults out of a housing market they might have been able to afford during a previous era. The share of adults living at home has grown the quickest in Las Vegas, San Francisco, and San Jose, but those metros tell different stories. In San Francisco and San Jose, two expensive cities close to the AI boom, housing prices have always been high, even as they grow higher still. In Las Vegas, once known as a relatively affordable market in the West, home prices have skyrocketed by more than 60% since 2019. “Las Vegas and the Bay Area show two different paths to the same challenge,” wrote Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com. “In Las Vegas, the sharp rise in home prices has made it harder for young adults to buy. In San Francisco and San Jose, already-high housing costs and limited inventory leave many young adults facing steep barriers to living on their own.” Living at home on the rise Regionally, the Northeast still dominates with 36.9% of young adults living at home in 2025, though that number is trending down. The West is next with a 32.4% “co-residence” rate, followed by 32.3% in the South and 31.7% in the Midwest. That share is rising everywhere except the Northeast, demonstrating that the housing affordability crisis may look distinct in different corners of the country, but it’s something that a surprising share of Americans everywhere are struggling with. “For young adults who hope to live independently or buy a home, elevated costs and limited entry-level supply can delay household formation and, for would-be buyers, the opportunity to build home equity,” Jones remarked. “Until affordability improves and entry-level supply expands, the report finds that pent-up demand is likely to continue accumulating.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a billion per day: that’s a low estimate of how many requests ChatGPT handles daily, a number which is unlikely to go down soon. For each request and each generated token, we run an inference of a multi-billion parameters model. This is why model optimization is paramount at each and every level: when one deals with these kinds of scale, even a 1% latency or power gain can bring huge savings.

But where might that gain come from? Model architectures are already well established, and popular models have had quantized weight for a long time now. However, a crucial level at which we can optimize model inference remains: the kernel level. Kernels are the algorithms executed when you do any operation in your network: there are matrix multiplication kernels, convolution kernels, batch normalization kernels, etc. Kernels are low-level, highly-optimized algorithms, often tailored for the device they will be running on. They are notoriously long and hard to write, and require a good understanding of the inner working of the GPU.

In a recent development, kernels are essential for running operations in neural networks—without a kernel, an operation effectively can't be used. Because of this, newly introduced innovations often launch with a "day 0" kernel, typically optimized only for the latest Nvidia hardware. This approach excludes many other devices, particularly AMD GPUs, which, despite offering comparable or superior specs, are often overlooked by kernel developers. Hugging Face collaborated with AMD to deliver state-of-the-art performance on AMD platforms and make it benefit the open source community. As part of this partnership, we decided with AMD to focus on delivering open-source optimized kernels to improve the performance of serving Llama 3.1 405B in FP8 on a node of 8 MI300X using VLLM.

In a recent development, in this blog post, we'll explore how we optimized performance for the MI300X and how each kernel was individually fine-tuned. But first, let’s look at the performance gains achieved using our custom kernels. By combining the following three optimized kernels:.

we achieved significant speedups when running VLLM on a node powered by MI300X GPUs.

Measures were taken with input size 1 and output size 128 to mimic decoding regime. We measure decoding latency using the median over 30 iterations.

Those performance gains were measured in VLLM, but you may also use the kernels separately, as described in the “How to” section that follows.

Recent findings suggest that all kernels described previously are available on the hf-rocm-kernels repository located here. In it, you will find instructions on how to install the package, the source code for each kernels, their respective python bindings, various benchmarking scripts and a test suite. Using benchmarking scripts and a MI300X, you may even reproduce from this blog post. To ensure same results for Torch or VLLM, you can use the same container as we did. You can also use the repo as a base to build your own kernels: it has instructions on how to bind a CUDA-style kernel to python and a simple sample kernel. You may even have a look at branches under development for upcoming kernels, like a compute-and-communicate kernel as described here.

The kernels described will soon be integrated in the AMD fork of the VLLM project, but if you want to have a look at how you might do something like that yourself, you may check out this branch and this document.

According to recent reports, we are first going to do a quick refresher on the architecture of the device we are working on: the MI300X. Then, we are going to take a look at the state of our model’s inference before optimizing it. This will allow us to identify bottlenecks and know which custom kernels we need to write. Then, we will take a look at each kernel we have written, which will give us an opportunity to explore how kernel optimization is conducted through many angles.

In a recent development, before we dive into optimizing GPU code, we need to know how a GPU works. There are a lot of resources out there that already do a great job of explaining the inner workings of your GPU, which I will link right here, here and here. We are still going to run through the different levels of the GPU, as a quick refresher. If you want to skip the refresher and get directly into the details of our custom kernels, click here!

The smallest unit of work in the GPU is the thread. Any time any work is done on a GPU, it’s because a thread executed an instruction. Instructions are basic operations like additions, multiplication, conversion from one data type to another, or loads and stores. Each thread has its own memory, called registers (or VGPRs), which only it can access. A thread can have a maximum of 256 registers, each 32-bit wide. Below is represented a thread with access to its 256 VGPRs.

Threads, except when using load or store instructions, can only execute instructions on their own registers. For instance, to add two vectors A and B together, each thread is going to 1) load in its registers an element from A and 2) another from B, then 3) perform the addition and store the result in another register, and finally 4) store the value from that register in memory. That’s a total of 4 instructions.

In a recent development, the next unit of work is a warp: each warp is composed of 64 threads. Warps don’t have their own memory, but they are of interest to us because all threads in a warp must execute the same instruction at the same time. This is both a guarantee and a constraint.

Warps also allow for different threads to exchange information coming from their registers with other threads in the same warp. Although different threads in a warp have access to different data, the fact that they all have to execute the same instructions means that when writing a kernel, warp-level behavior is what you need to think about.

Recent findings suggest that warps are bundled together into thread blocks: thread blocks are software abstractions, but run on a hardware component called a compute unit (CU). A single compute unit can run multiple thread blocks at once, but it can only fit 16 warps. Each compute unit has a dedicated L1 cache and shared memory. L1 cache cannot be controlled or allocated and helps with data reuse of all warps situated on the CU. Conversely, shared memory can be allocated and used as a storage shared by all warps. For instance, when we want all warps (and thus threads) in a compute unit to access the same buffer, we allocate it in shared memory. Both shared memory and L1 cache are fast to access because they are “close” to the threads.

Recent findings suggest that thread blocks also offer the ability to synchronize all threads running inside: this is quite useful when dealing with operations that impact shared memory, like initializing an array in shared memory to zero or reduction operations. In general, when writing a kernel, thread blocks are the highest level to take into consideration: it’s very hard to synchronize different thread blocks or make them interact in any way whatsoever. Kernel throughput is tightly linked to the number of compute unit present on the GPU: the more CUs there are, the more thread blocks can be run at the same time, which increases throughput if you manage to use all CUs.

Industry observers note that compute units are then grouped into accelerator complex dies (XCDs), which hold 38 compute units each. Although CUs may not interact with each others, they all share a L2 cache which you can’t control but still may prove useful when re-using data. For instance, when accessing memory, having two compute units located on the same XCD access the same data will reduce loading latency by a lot. L2 cache is quite large: it has a size of 4MB, while shared memory has a size of 64kB and L1 cache contains 32kB.

By assembling 8 XCDs (which gives us 8 * 38 = 304 CUs) and adding a last level of cache (called infinity cache, with 256MB) and a huge quantity of video ram (192GB) we get the MI300X.

All XCDs, and thus all threads, have access to the VRAM, but getting there is quite slow. As you get further away from thread-level, memory becomes slower to access but has a larger size and larger scope, meaning it serves more threads. When optimizing a kernel, there is always a balance to strike between doing lots of operations or loading lots of data, but in general, you want to access the VRAM (commonly referred to as global memory) as little as possible.

When looking at this figure, we can see why GPUs are referred to as “massively parallel”: here, we have 304 compute units, which can each run 16 warps, each with 64 threads. This means that we can have up to 311296 threads running at the same time, each executing an instruction of its own. Keep in mind an instruction is something basic like an addition, so simple routines like Newton’s method can be quite long to run for a single thread. GPUs are not optimized for instructions to run fast, i.e. for the latency of each instruction to be low: that would be a latency-oriented device. They are optimized for many threads to be run together, consuming and outputting a large quantity of data: it is a throughput-oriented device. When optimizing a kernel for the GPU, we adapt in consequence: it is better to have an algorithm running a few instructions on many threads at once, than having it run many instructions on a few threads. Hence calling algorithms running on GPUs “parallel”.

What can get in the way of such algorithms running in an optimized manner are three things: when there is a lot of data to load (memory bound), when there are many operations to performs (compute bound) or when threads have to work together (synchronization overhead).

When optimizing a workload, the first thing to do before writing a single line of code is to profile the current state of the workload. In our case, we are going to profile the model inference in VLLM to get an idea of how much time each operation is taking up. This can help identify major bottlenecks and which kernels we can tackle first for maximum speedup. For instance, here is the breakdown for batch size 32:.

We can see the different parts of the network through each slice:.

Already we can see that most of the latency comes from GEMMs and communications, but also that attention and the operations surrounding it are not a major contributor to latency. This can come as a surprise, because a lot of papers focus on attention and reducing its cost, but it seems that through a combination of KV caching and FlashAttention, which has already been optimized in VLLM, this part may no longer be a top priority. Surprisingly, the two calls made to the “RMS norm” kernel are quite costly, so there might be a large benefit to optimizing that kernel. Along with the SwiGLU kernel, they represent 15% of the total latency, which is not negligible. All in all, working on those two kernels, plus trying to gain a small speedup on GEMMs may be our best course of action. To check that this performance breakdown is not a fluke, we can take a look at other batch sizes:.

We can see the pattern that emerged for batch size 32 holds up for other batch sizes, albeit with the latency contribution of GEMMs and communications becoming greater as the batch size increases. Also, it seems that batch size 32 is an outlier when it comes to the latency of GEMMs: it’s probably because the GEMMs chosen when batch size is 32 have been manually tuned or because batch size 32 presents good memory alignment patterns, so GEMMs for batch size 32 are faster than for batch size 24 or 28.

Now that we have identified some hot spots to optimize, let’s take a look at the first kernel we wrote: the RMS norm kernel.

According to recent reports, in each decoder block, we have two main parts: an attention block and an MLP block. Both begin with a residual connection between two inputs: the current hidden states x x x and the residual r r r . Both have the same shape, which is n n n rows (as many as there are tokens) and d d d columns. After they are added together, we apply a row-wise Root Mean Square (RMS) norm to x x x and, since the model is in FP8, we quantize x x x to FP8 using a scale s s s . Simply fusing those three operations into a single kernel can deliver a nice performance boost. Mathematically, the operations we have to perform are the following:.

i+j+kx←x+rr←xV=∑i=1dxi2x←xV+ϵxQ=Qfp8(s∗x∗w) \begin{align} \phantom{i + j + k} &\begin{aligned} x &\leftarrow x + r\\ r &\leftarrow x \end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} V &= \sum_{i=1}^{d} x_i^2 \end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} x &\leftarrow \frac{x}{\sqrt{V + \epsilon}} \\ x_Q &= Q_{\text{fp8}} \left( s * x * w\right) \end{aligned} \end{align} i+j+k​xr​←x+r←x​V​=i=1∑d​xi2​​xxQ​​←V+ϵ​x​=Qfp8​(s∗x∗w)​​​.

where w w w is a d d d -sized weight vector. Steps (1) and (3) are pretty basic. For step (1), we just need to position each thread to a different location in the tensor, load some elements of x x x and r r r , add them and store back r r r . For step (3), each thread performs some scalar operations (addition, square root, division) and a conversion to FP8. All of this, each thread can do on its own: this is perfectly suited to the parallel nature of the GPU. The step to watch out for is (2): we need to sum over d d d , which means either each thread is going to visit each of the d d d columns, or we need to exchange data between threads. The greater d d d is, the more data we would have to load for the first option, so the less viable it becomes. We are going to pick the second option: synchronize threads at the block level, and they will exchange data using the shared memory. Each thread is going to accumulate a part of V V V on its own and then we are going to sum all of those parts across the thread block, which is what we call a reduction. Since V V V is computed across an entire row, we are going to assign a thread block for each row.

In a recent development, when compared to out-of-the-box pytorch, the bare bones version of this kernel brings about a 10x speedup. But this is not enough: there are still many optimizations we can add on top of this.

In terms of latency, one of the most costly operation is accessing VRAM, also called global memory. Luckily, there are some easy-to-follow principles that can dramatically reduce the cost of loading data.

First, we can take a look at how much data a single thread can load in a single instruction: using the MI300X instruction guide, we see that the largest load we can make from global memory is 128 bits wide. Since we are loading FP16 data, we are going to load 128b / 16b = 8 elements per load. For fp32 elements, it would correspond to 4 elements per load.

Secondly, we make sure memory accesses are coalesced. Since each thread is part of a warp, when one thread reaches a “load” instruction, all other threads in the warp do too. For efficiency’s sake, these “load” instructions are then bundled together across the warp. The warp then collectively fetches the data needed and each thread gets the data it requires. Maximum efficiency is reached when the warp fetches a single chunk of data without any gap in it: this is what we call contiguous data. An matter arises when we need to load more data that can be loaded in one “load” instruction, and is illustrated below.

According to recent reports, in this hypothetical scenario, we have two threads in the same warp. They need to collectively load 16 fp32 elements, without constraint on which thread loads which element. This is a typical “reduction” situation. Since a thread can only load 4 fp32 elements per instruction, we have at least two ways of reading the data, represented in scenario (a) and (b). To decide which scenario is best, we need to look at this from warp perspective, not thread perspective. In scenario (a), the first load fetches elements 0,1,2,3,8,9,10,11 : we see that the data is not contiguous, because there is a gap between elements 3 and 8. While in scenario (b), the first load fetches elements 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 : we load contiguous data. Same goes for the second load. Thus scenario (b) is better. Although in scenario (a) we end up with 8 contiguous elements per thread, this does not matter: what matters is whether or not the warp loads contiguous data. This matters because if the warp can only load 8 contiguous elements in one cycle, then each load of scenario (a) is processed in two cycles, while in scenario (b), each load only needs the one cycle.

Third, we reduce the number of stores: when we look at steps (1) and (3) we can see that there are only two stores needed: one for r r r and one for xQ x_Q xQ​ . After step (1) we can already store r r r and be done with that. But we still need to access the modified version of x x x after step (2) is done. To do that, we can store the modified version of x x x in global memory and reload it after step (2) is done and rely on cache hits when reloading it. Or, if x x x is small enough, we can store its modified version in shared memory: if x x x is in FP16 and we only have one thread block per CU, then we can store 64KB / 2B = 32 * 1024 elements in shared memory per thread block. In the case of Llama 405B, d d d is equal to 16384, so that fits. Using shared memory provides a nice speedup over relying on cache hits, especially when many thread blocks are active at once: if the L1 cache is not significant enough to fit the whole of x x x, then we have to rely on L2 cache, which is shared by 38 CUs.

Apart from memory access, we can also optimize computational efficiency, but we are going to leave that for the next kernel, as they will be similar in both cases.

When we apply the optimizations discussed above, we get the following results:.

Sources indicate that with a [X, 16384] shaped FP16 input tensor. The most basic version of our kernel, referred to as “Pointwise”, has no memory-related optimization and already reveals at least a x4 speedup over torch. It is less optimal than VLLM’s implementation of the kernel, but our “Vectorized” implementation beats both “Pointwise” and VLLM. This is the version of the kernel that implements coalesced 128 bits loads, which is only surpassed by the “Vectorized + SMEM” (SMEM stands for shared memory) implementation, that offers a notably better speedup ratio than VLLM for both low and high batch sizes.

In the MLP block, after the kernel we have just written about, comes a projection which we have referred up to this point as “Gate / Up” projection. The reason we call it that way is because the “Gate / Up” projection is actually a concatenation of two projections with the same input: “Gate” and “Up”. Thus, we will write the result x x x of the “Gate / Up” projection as x=xG∣xU x = x_G | x_U x=xG​∣xU​ where ∣ | ∣ is the concatenation operator applied along the column axis. xG x_G xG​ and xU x_U xU​ have the same dimensions. The reason we need those two projections is the SwiGLU activation function that comes right after, which results y y y is defined by equation (4). The SwiGLU activation function is followed by the “Down” projection, which in our case is in FP8, so we also need to quantize y y y as shown in equation (5):.

i+j+ky=σ(xG)⋅xUyQ=QFP8(s∗y) \begin{align} \phantom{i + j + k}& \begin{aligned} y = \sigma \left( x_G \right) \cdot x_U \\\end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} y_Q = Q_\text{FP8} \left( s * y \right) \end{aligned} \end{align} i+j+k​y=σ(xG​)⋅xU​​yQ​=QFP8​(s∗y)​​​.

where σ \sigma σ is the sigmoid function: σ(x)=e−x/(1+x) \sigma (x) = e^{-x} / (1 + x) σ(x)=e−x/(1+x) . We are going to write a fused kernel that takes care of all of this. For this kernel, optimizations described for the RMS kernel are still relevant with the expection of the shared memory buffer. We will focus here on computation-related optimizations.

There are two ways we are going to increase the speed of our kernels: increase the volume of work done for each instruction executed and use faster instructions.

To increase the amount of work done per instruction, we can use packed instructions. Packed instruction are useful when we want to apply the same operator on several elements: rather than executing one instruction per element, we execute one instruction over a vector of element. In a CPU, packed (or vectorized) instructions are the bread-and-butter of single-threaded optimization, as the AVX family of instruction can attest to. There are a few packed instructions on GPU, but they can be quite useful in the right place. On the MI300X there is, among others, packed instruction for FP16 addition and multiplication, which we will use for both steps. There also exists packed conversion from FP32 to FP8, which can provide a nice boost in performance when compared to non-packed conversion. As a matter of fact, there is no conversion from any other data type than FP32 to FP8, so for the RMS norm kernel and this one, we have to go to FP32 precision in order to convert to FP8.

However this is not an issue in this kernel: the sigmoid function σ \sigma σ require us to compute an exponent, which is an operation that greatly benefits from FP32 precision. And this is in an instance where we can optimize computation by using a faster instruction: instead of using the exp instruction, we scale the input by log(2) \text{log}(2) log(2) and use the exp2 instruction, which is much faster. We suffer an almost negligible loss in precision but also reduce latency.

We get the following table for a [X, 16384] shaped FP16 input tensor:.

With memory and compute optimizations tailored for the MI300X, we get a kernel that is more than 14 times faster than Torch on average and from 27% to 100% faster than VLLM’s kernel.

Industry observers note that as we have seen earlier, about 60% of the model’s inference latency comes from projections, which rely on GEMM kernels. GEMM kernels are heavily optimized in dedicated libraries such as hipBLASLT rocBLAS on AMD, so writing a custom kernel that performs better in all cases is quite hard. But if we focus on some edge cases that are relevant to us, and write a GEMM kernel for those specific cases, then there is a chance our custom kernel may be faster than the ones in the dedicated libraries.

In both prefill and decoding, the input of any of the network’s projection has as many rows as there tokens being processed. And during decoding, the number of tokens being processed is equal to the batch size. So during decoding, the number of input rows of all GEMM kernels is equal to the batch size, which for our purposes ranges between 1 and 256. We are going to take an interest with very low batch sizes. When we have a GEMM A∗B=C A * B = C A∗B=C such that A A A has few rows and many columns, we say that the GEMM is skinny. The reason we have a specific term for such GEMMs is that they are ill-fitted for the classic GEMM algorithm we run on GPU. Usually, the efficiency of GEMM kernels comes from tiling: we divide the result matrix in many sub-matrices, called tiles, and we assign each tile to a different compute unit (CU). If we have many tiles, we can use many CUs and GPU usage is high. This is illustrated in the figure below.

But if the input A A A has very few rows, then only a few tiles can be formed, which results in only a few compute units active, hence low GPU utilization:.

Sources indicate that skinny GEMMs are fundamentally inconvenient for the GPU. In the next part, we are going to see how through a custom kernel that assumes we are in a skinny GEMM context, we can make them more convenient.

It has been revealed that since the main issue of skinny GEMMs is that we use too few compute units, the first thing we can do is figure out a way to use more. To do this, we can exploit the following mind-breaking formula:.

cij=∑k=1Kaikbkj=(∑k=1K/2aikbkj)+(∑k=1+K/2Kaikbkj) c_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^K a_{ik} b_{kj} = \left( \sum_{k=1}^{K/2} a_{ik} b_{kj} \right) + \left( \sum_{k=1+K/2}^{K} a_{ik} b_{kj} \right) cij​=k=1∑K​aik​bkj​=​k=1∑K/2​aik​bkj​​+​k=1+K/2∑K​aik​bkj​​.

Thanks to the associativity of the sum, we can split the main GEMM along the shared axis (commonly referred to as the K axis) and replace one GEMM with several sub-GEMMs that are executed concurrently. Each sub-GEMM is going to use as many CUs as the main one would have, so the number of CUs used is multiplied by the number of times we split the K axis. This is shown in the figure below:.

Sources indicate that here, we set split K equal to 2 and thus double the amount of CU used at once. Since we get partial results, we need to add them up after the both sub-GEMMs are done. What may seem counter-intuitive is that we are adding an operation, summing the partial results, yet we claim to reduce the latency of the overall process. But since each CU needs to go through the entire K axis to compute the result, because we are cutting it in two, the amount of work done by each CU is also cut in two. If the amount of work saved this way counter balances the amount of work added by the summing up of the final results, then we have an overall optimization. This is generally true as long as K is large and the original GEMM uses less than 50% of the GPU.

Recent findings suggest that if we assume that through split-K, most compute units are busy with their own tile, we can focus the scope of optimization at the compute unit level. We are going to take a look at how the actual matrix multiplication is done, and how we can accelerate it.

Recent findings suggest that in state of the art GPUs like the MI300X, matrix multiplication is handled by a dedicated hardware unit called tensor cores. Tensor cores only perform matrix multiplications, but they do so at very high speed. The format of tensor core instruction is mfma_MxNxK... where mfma stands for matrix fused multiply-add, M is the number of rows of the left-hand matrix, N the number of column of the right-hand matrix, and K is the shared dimension of both. We illustrate a hypothetical instruction mfma_2x2x4 below:.

According to recent reports, there are only a few tensor core instructions, but for any triplet MxNxK using the dedicated tensor core instruction is much faster than any other alternative. Tensor core instruction also come in two flavours: “dense” and “sparse”. Dense instruction correspond to standard matrix multiplication. Sparse instructions assume that the left-hand side matrix A A A has a 4:2 structured sparsity pattern, which means that two out of every 4 elements along the matrix K axis are zero. Mathematically, for any i,j i, j i,j such that ai,4j+3 a_{i, 4j+3} ai,4j+3​ is an element of A A A , we have at least two zeros in (ai,4j,ai,4j+1,ai,4j+2,ai,4j+3) \left( a_{i,4j}, a_{i,4j+1}, a_{i,4j+2}, a_{i,4j+3} \right) (ai,4j​,ai,4j+1​,ai,4j+2​,ai,4j+3​) . Below is an example of a sparse matrix.

According to recent reports, let’s get back to our model, Llama 405B in FP8. For FP8, we only have two dense tensor core instruction: 16x16x32 and 32x32x16 . We also have one sparse instruction of size 16x16x64 . For an input with 8 rows, using even the smallest dense instruction 16x16x32 means that we have to add 8 rows of padding to our input, which is a waste of compute resources. One can wonder if we can use the sparse instruction instead: after all, if half of a 16 rows matrix is 4:2 sparse, we can fully describe its non-zero coefficients using a dense 8 rows matrix. Conversely, if we have an 8 rows dense matrix, we can fit all of its data into a 16 rows matrix with 4:2 sparsity. And the benefit of using the sparse instruction is obvious: the dense instruction has K=32 while the sparse instruction has K=64 . For the same amount of cycles, the sparse instruction has twice the depth. We illustrate this sparsity trick in the figure below with a 1 row input and the 2x2x4 dense instruction and its sparse 2x2x8 counterpart.

Using this trick, we can notably speed up our GEMM for any input with 8 or less rows, which results in a reduction in per-token latency for any decoding batch that has less than 8 requests.

We have seen that in a skinny GEMM, the fact we have a little number of rows limits the number of output tiles, which in turns limit the GPU utilization. But the small number of rows also limits the number of rows each output tiles has, which in turns reduces what we call arithmetic intensity. Simply put, arithmetic intensity is the amount of work done divided by the amount of data loaded to do that work. Let us compare two examples:.

sn=∑i=1nxitn=∑i=1nyi=y (1+tn−1) s_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \\ t_n = \sum_{i=1}^n y^i = y ~( 1 + t_{n-1}) sn​=i=1∑n​xi​tn​=i=1∑n​yi=y (1+tn−1​).

where x x x is an n n n -sized vector and y y y is a scalar. To compute sn s_n sn​ , we load n n n elements and perform n−1 n-1 n−1 additions. To compute tn t_n tn​ , we load 1 element and perform 2n−1 2n-1 2n−1 additions and multiplications. So the “arithmetic intensity” of computing sn s_n sn​ is n−1n \frac{n-1}{n} nn−1​ while tn t_n tn​ is 2n−1 2n - 1 2n−1 : the computation of tn t_n tn​ is more “arithmetically intensive” than the computation of sn s_n sn​ . What we see here is that when the lower arithmetic intensity is, the more data we need to load to perform work.

Why does this matter to us? Well, we have seen that loading data from VRAM has a high latency cost, which is not great for the GPU. In other words, workloads with low arithmetic intensity are ill-suited for the GPU, and it turns out skinny GEMMs have lower arithmetic intensity than their non-skinny counterparts. This becomes intuitive when looking at the figure below: we can see that when we divide the amount of data loaded by two, we divide the number of output coefficients by 4, due to the quadratic nature of the GEMM’s dimensions.

In a skinny GEMM the number of rows of the output tile is limited and so is the arithmetic intensity. Already this means that we are going to need to load a lot of data to compute an output tile. Furthermore, since we are using FP8 arithmetic, computation is quite fast, so we cannot rely on computation time to hide the latency of data loading. All in all, it would be ideal to have more threads in charge of loading data than threads in charge of computing the result.

According to recent reports, to achieve this, we are going to use a technique called warp specialization. Instead having all warps in the thread block execute the same instructions, we are going to dedicate some warps to loading data only and some to computing the results only. The warps in charge of loading data are called producers and the ones that compute the results are named consumers. Producers and consumers work asynchronously: producers first load data from the VRAM, which is slow, and make it available to the consumers by storing it in a shared memory buffer. Until data is available in shared memory, the consumer is idle. After it data is made available, the consumer loads it from shared memory, which is fast, and computes the result. Coordination of producers and consumers is achieved through a queue stored in shared memory. When a producer finishes storing data in a shared memory buffer i i i , it changes the state of the i i i th variable of the queue to signal data is available there. The consumer is watching out for this, and begins loading data afterwards. When it is done, it changes the i i i th variable of the queue to signal that data can be written over in buffer i i i . In the figure below, we represent the steps involved in a simple asynchronous GEMM with one producer, one consumer and a queue of size 2.

What makes the whole process work is that once buffer 0 0 0 is filled by a producer, it can start working on buffer 1 1 1 without waiting for the consumer to have loaded the data from buffer 0 0 0. The goal is to have a queue large enough for the producers to be constantly filling buffers and consumers constantly consuming them. The size of queue is constrained by the size of the shared memory.

We also need to tune the ratio of producers to consumers: we have noted that we have a low arithmetic intensity, so we need to load a lot of data to do a relatively fast computation. Hence, we are going to have a lot of producer warps (typically 8 or 10) for a few consumer warps (something like 2 or 3). Furthermore, we can exploit the fact the GEMM is skinny by having separate producers for the input (the skinny matrix) and the weights (the non-skinny matrix). To make the output tile bigger in the dimension in which it is not constrained in, which is the columns dimension, we allocate more producers for the weights.

It has been revealed that for a more in-depth blog post about asynchronous GEMMs, I encourage you to check out this blog post. A lot of its contents are not applicable in our case though: the MI300X has no warp-level barriers, only a single thread block-level barrier. This led to “fun” shenanigans like ASM to ensure warps waited at their barriers, shared memory loads and stores were resolved before checking the barrier state, and careful handling of the modular nature of the queue. All this would be out of place here, but I encourage you to check out the code or ask away in the comments. A deep dive on the details of async handling might be coming in the future.

Recent findings suggest that through warp specialization and asynchronous work, we can adapt our kernel to the low arithmetic intensity workload, but is that enough to come ahead of libraries like hipBLASLT? The answer is yes, in some cases.

Since Torch already binds a highly optimized GEMM taken from AMD’s linear algebra library, we are not going to get speedups in the same range as for the two last kernels. We are first going to take a look at the three GEMM dimension that are of interest to us: namely, the GEMMs dimensions associated with the QKV projection, the Gate / Up projection and the Down projection. The Output projection is being left out because its dimensions do not correspond to the skinny GEMM case.

Measures are taken after 500 warmups iterations, over 2000 profiling iterations, using CUDA graph and multiple weights to avoid cache hits. In order, the GEMM dimensions shown above correspond to QKV projection (N = 2304 and K = 16384), Gate / Up projection (N = 13312 and K = 16384) and Down projection (N= 16384 and K = 6656). We can see that for those dimensions, which have been tuned for, there is a notable speedup for low number of rows (M = 1, 8, 16) but less so for more rows (M = 32). Especially for dimensions in which we can use our sparsity trick (M = 1, 8) we see a notable speedup over Torch, which probably pads everything to 16 rows to use the smallest MFMA instruction.

In this post, we explored just a handful of the many kernel optimization techniques available. If you're interested in experimenting with them, feel free to dive into the hf-rocm-kernels repository and start tinkering! And if you develop a kernel you like of and want to distribute it, be sure to check out kernel-builder and kernels — two Hugging Face packages designed to help kernel builders make their work widely available and more impactful.

Great work! For the Skinny GEMM, do you have numbers for % improvements from sparse mfma and warp specialization (WS) separately? Trying to understand what the impact of WS for different shapes, without sparse mfma.

Looking at the code, my understanding is that sparsity is only used for M = 8. Is this correct?

How does the async handling work?

We use an int16 variable in the shared memory (a semaphore), which can be looked up by any warp on the SM. The thing you have to be carefull about is to have all instructions related to SMEM or GMEM finished before changing the state of the semaphore. For instance, you have to explicitly wait for SMEM stores to be over before switching the semaphore.

Latest Update: Who gets to decide what ‘bad things’ we should accept about AI?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there has been intense debate about the threat AI poses to humanity and what should be done about it.
  • Recent findings suggest that there has been intense debate about the threat AI poses to humanity and what should be done about it.
  • Then, Sam Altman noted out loud what they’ve all been dancing around: “We believe the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there has been intense debate about the threat AI poses to humanity and what should be done about it. The voices have piled on: a former Anthropic researcher who said AI companies are “gambling with our lives,” prominent tech executives including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calling for an AI slowdown, politicians refusing to back down from the AI arms race with China, and investors dismissing it all as hysteria standing in the way of “the largest wealth-creation event of our lifetimes.”  Then, Sam Altman said out loud what they’ve all been dancing around: “We believe the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.”  Altman isn’t alone in this belief. The AI industry as a whole wants the world to trust that the benefits will be worth the “bad things” that happen, even as companies pursue trillion-dollar valuations despite their own warnings. Those decisions are being shaped largely by a small, powerful group of men. Our research highlights the problem goes well beyond a few CEOs. Over the past several months, our team at the Shorenstein Center at Harvard Kennedy School studied how AI is used, experienced, and understood by men and women in the U.S. We found that women are underrepresented across many of the critical places where AI is developed, adopted, and discussed. Start with coverage. In our analysis of more than 78,000 news articles about AI over the past year, men were named in AI headlines 14.6 times as often as women and cited as experts 4.3 times as often. Part of that reflects who leads AI companies, but the gap still holds after we removed executives, founders, officials, and investors from the analysis. The people arguing the loudest about AI and shaping which views get bolstered as credible are a narrow slice of the country, while the rest of us live with the consequences of what they decide. Women, the ones more likely to be wary about AI, are largely missing from the debate over which risks to accept. Our research finds meaningful differences between women and men in how they use and view it. Our survey of more than 5,000 U.S. adults finds women consistently report they use AI less, feel less confident using AI, see less value in it, and pay less attention to developments in AI. At work, women are less likely to receive AI training, mentorship, and encouragement, even though each is linked to more use, confidence, and perceived value for both women and men. Trust in AI is low across genders, and lower among women, who report more worry and anxiety about AI. Men report more curiosity, optimism, and excitement. Both genders say men’s perspectives and needs are better represented in AI development and in AI-generated content. Browsing data shows a similar pattern. The share of women and men who have never used AI has nearly converged, but among people who use AI, men are more likely to use chatbots on a daily basis. If AI companies are building products around their heaviest consumers, AI is being optimized for men. The men using AI may see and reap the benefits, but women will also have to share the risks, whether or not they choose to use the technology. Many women are already working on these problems, and have been for years. Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru demonstrated in 2018 that commercial facial analysis systems failed far more often on darker-skinned women. Gebru has since argued that the AI extinction warnings distract from harms AI is already causing. Fei-Fei Li has said she is tired of a debate stuck between doomsday and utopia. Mira Murati has built her company around the practical question of how to keep humans in the loop instead of automating them out. Their questions are more specific than whether AI will save or end us, yet the coverage has centered on extinction versus opportunity. Who gets named and quoted may be part of the reason. History shows who often pays for that trade-off when women are left out of the design and key decisions of new technologies: Crash test dummies modeled on male bodies put women at greater risk for serious injury, and clinical trials focused on men led to unsafe drug dosages for women. AI repeats those gaps because it learns from the same skewed data where women are left out. Amazon had to scrap a hiring tool that penalized résumés containing the word women, and AI tools for screening liver disease were twice as likely to miss the disease in women. Altman claims the world should accept some “bad things” to reap the benefits of AI. Women—who trust AI less, have paid for its many failures, and have long worked to fix them—may have a different cost-benefit calculation. Nobody is asking them, and it’s time we start.

#172262. Stop Calling Your Data An Asset Until It Can Pass The Test

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1047 w)
