AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Googleblog ↗ Open Full Page

Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (400 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who notes they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight.
  • They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules.
  • Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who notes they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight. The agent can read the file and send email, so it fulfills the user request. Semantic governance policies, available in Preview in Gemini platform, enable enterprises to govern their agents and provide guardrails to stop that call before it runs. They check each tool call an agent proposes against what the user asked for and against rules you write in plain language.

Permissions alone can't catch this. They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules. A model can also be talked out of the rules in its system instructions, by a user with a good reason, or by a document telling it to do something nobody asked for, a technique called indirect prompt injection. So the check has to sit outside the agent. Semantic governance policies are enforced through a policy enforcement point, such as Agent Gateway, alongside the agent governance controls we expanded in October, so policies stay separate from your agent's code.

Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:.

A call has to pass both checks to run.

According to recent reports, today, the policy enforcement point that Semantic governance policies support is Agent Gateway. You need to configure your agent so all your agent egress traffic goes through Agent Gateway, facilitating traffic between your agent and its model. When the model responds with a tool call, Agent Gateway sends the proposed call to the Semantic governance policy engine for evaluation before the response reaches your agent.

In the policy engine, an LLM judge evaluates the proposed call against the conversation so far, the agent's system instructions and tool descriptions, and your policies.

Recent findings suggest that if the call passes, the response reaches your agent unchanged. If it doesn't, the engine replaces the response's content, tool calls included, with a configurable denial message, so the call never runs. Either way, the verdict and the judge's rationale go to Cloud Logging in your project. Responses that contain only text, such as an answer, a blueprint, or a question back to the user, aren't evaluated, because they take no action.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AirTag-like trackers for Android and iPhone are everywhere nowadays, but Kodak’s newly introduced SlideTag steps it up with a built-in E-Ink display that can show off your photos, widgets, and more along with being able to track down your items.

Industry observers note that compatible with both the Android Find Hub and Apple Find My networks, the Kodak SlideTag is a tracker inspired by the golden era of Kodak photography. The tracker is built by Reto, the same company that built the Kodak Chamera keychain digital camera.

Industry observers note that slideTag’s premise is relatively simple. You get a tracker with an E-Ink display and a frame in one of eight styles inspired by classic 35mm slides. Those styles are sold in a blind box format, meaning you don’t know what you’re getting until you open the box (unless you buy the full set). There’s also a ninth style that only highlights up in one out of every 64 boxes.

It has been revealed that the E-Ink display can show six-color versions of your photos, or it can display things like lists, calendars, and more. There’s enough storage on the tracker for a 12-photo slideshow, synced through the Kodak Memory Link app on Android and iOS.

When one person chats with a local model, it barely matters which server you run. On one RTX 3090 with the same model file, Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp wrote text within about 10 percent of each other, because all three run llama.cpp underneath. That changes when your app sends several requests at once. With four requests, the best setup produced more than three times as much text as the worst, and the cause was a default setting, not the engine. With 32 requests, vLLM produced 2.5 times as much text as the best llama.cpp setup I tested.

This article puts those numbers side by side and indicates which setting to change for your app.

Industry observers note that I ran every test on one machine. The full write-ups, with every command and the raw results, are on homebrewserver.club.

Every server got the same requests:.

Sources indicate that ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp loaded the exact same GGUF files, checked by SHA-256. vLLM cannot run GGUF files well, so it loaded a 4-bit AWQ file of the same model (9.1 GB). Answer quality was not compared.

Sources indicate that the tests ran between 8 and 16 November 2026, and speeds on this machine varied by a few percent from one day to the next. Treat a gap under about 5% as a tie. All of this is one consumer GPU and one model family, so read the numbers as a guide to how the servers behave, not as a ranking for your hardware.

This is the short prompt with a 512-token answer.

Sources indicate that ollama and LM Studio both start llama.cpp's llama-server program for each model they load. Ollama has done this since version 0.30, and a comment in its source code says so. On Linux, LM Studio's CUDA runtime is a folder with llama.cpp libraries and a llama-server binary.

Ollama logs the command it starts when you set OLLAMA_DEBUG=1. When llama.cpp was started by hand with that exact command, in a run next to Ollama, its speed matched Ollama's within 1%. So Ollama adds no speed cost of its own. LM Studio was 5 to 10% slower in this test. The test did not separate whether that came from its llama.cpp build or its other start options.

For one user, the gap between Ollama and LM Studio was about 0.4 s on a 512-token answer from the 9B model. You would notice it in long answers, and hardly in a chat window.

It has been revealed that A web app rarely sends one request at a time. A chat page, a background summary job and an agent can all call the same model at the same moment. The next test sent four requests at once, each asking for 256 tokens, and measured the total output per second.

A slot is one request that the server works on at the same time as others. llama-server sets the number of slots with -np (short for --parallel), and Ollama and LM Studio pass their own setting through to it.

With one slot, the server answers the four requests one after another, so the total stays at the speed of a single request. That is Ollama's default. With four slots, the server puts the four requests through the model together, and the total rose to more than twice that of one slot. That is the default in LM Studio and llama.cpp. vLLM was the fastest at four requests, but it was tested only with the 9B model. Its lead grows with more requests, as the section after next highlights.

For your app, this means that the fourth user of a default Ollama server waits for the first three answers to finish before their own answer starts.

According to recent reports, the obvious fix is OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4. It worked for the 9B model, though in one of three rounds Ollama still answered at the speed of a single request. With the 27B model, it made Ollama slower than its default.

In a recent development, the cause is how each server sizes the context, the memory that holds each request's prompt and answer. Ollama picks the context from the GPU's memory: 32,768 tokens on a 24 GB card, according to its docs. With four slots, it gives each slot its own 32,768 tokens, so it started llama-server with a 131,072-token context. The Ollama FAQ says the memory needed grows with the number of parallel requests multiplied by the context length.

That context did not fit next to the 27B model in 24 GB. ollama ps revealed 16% of the model on the CPU, and the total speed fell to 33.1 tokens per second.

LM Studio and llama.cpp handle it differently. Their four slots share one pool of context:.

Sources indicate that the price of LM Studio's default is a short context. Four requests sharing 8,192 tokens leave little room for long documents or a long chat history. If your app sends long prompts, load the model with a larger context.

In a recent development, in Ollama, setting a smaller context with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH next to OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL should avoid the spill to the CPU. The test did not try this, so measure it on your own card.

The last test went further, from 1 to 32 requests at once, with the 9B model. It compared vLLM, a server built to serve one model to many users, with llama.cpp at its defaults and with more slots. Ollama and LM Studio were tested only up to four requests, so they are not in this table.

All figures are total tokens per second.

With its defaults, llama-server chose four slots by itself, so it worked on four requests and queued the rest. Its total stayed near 330 tokens per second from 4 requests to 32. Setting -np 16 or -np 32 roughly doubled the total at 16 requests.

Recent findings suggest that vLLM's lead came from each request running faster inside a large batch. At 32 requests, each vLLM request generated about 61 tokens per second, against about 27 on llama.cpp with 32 slots. vLLM's README names the two techniques behind this: PagedAttention, which stores each request's working memory in small blocks, and continuous batching, which adds fresh requests to the batch the GPU is already working on.

Recent findings suggest that total output tells you how much work the server does. The wait for the first word tells you how the app feels to the user behind the last request:.

Sources indicate that for a web app, that is 22.5 seconds of spinner before any text appears. Long prompts make every wait longer, on both servers. With eight requests of about 4,120 tokens each, the last request waited 7.9 s on vLLM and 8.8 s on llama.cpp with 32 slots.

If you set the slots yourself, the llama-server README lists three options that work together:.

If you run an older llama.cpp, upgrade first. Four requests at once ran 14 to 22% faster on v1.0.0 than on the build from five days earlier, while one request stayed the same. The most likely reason is a new CUDA kernel in v1.0 for steps of 2 to 24 tokens on RTX 30-series and newer cards.

vLLM's throughput comes with two costs that matter on a shared machine.

It reserves most of the GPU. By default, vLLM takes 92% of the card's memory before it loads anything, and fills what the model does not need with cache. With a desktop and a browser holding about 2 GiB, vLLM refused to start:.

Setting --gpu-memory-utilization 0.6 alone was not enough with this model, because the default limit of 256 sequences needed more cache than fit. Adding --max-num-seqs 32 fixed it. With both settings, vLLM held 12.7 GiB and kept the same speeds. llama.cpp works the other way: it sizes its cache from -c and -np and never asked for more than 15.1 GiB in this test.

In a recent development, it starts slowly. llama-server answered requests 2 to 5 s after its container started. vLLM compiles the model before it serves anything. That took 72 s with its compile cache already on disk, and 173 s on the first start without it. Changing a vLLM argument triggered a fresh compile.

It also needs a different model file. vLLM loads Hugging Face safetensors, so a 4-bit model is a separate AWQ or GPTQ upload. The AWQ file here was 9.1 GB against 5.7 GB for the GGUF, because its recipe leaves some layers unquantized. Check the file size, not only "4-bit", when you size a model for your card.

All four servers have an OpenAI-compatible API under /v1, so the same client code works with each one. You change the base URL and the model name. These are the ports used in the tests:.

In Node.js with the openai package, that looks like the sketch below. The measurements came from a Python test client, and this snippet was not part of them:.

Qwen3.5 thinks before it answers unless you turn it off. The tests sent "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} in the request body to vLLM and llama.cpp.

According to recent reports, none of the servers asked for a password in these tests. llama-server also warned at start-up that its CORS rule allowed all origins. Bind the port to 127.0.0.1, as in the table, and set --api-key on llama.cpp or vLLM if anything else on your network can reach it.

Sources indicate that before you choose, count how many requests your app really sends at the same moment. Log the timestamps for a day, or count the parallel calls your agent makes per user action. If that number is one, any of these servers will do. If it is four or more, the slot setting will change your consumers' wait more than the choice of engine.

Sources indicate that not for one request with the same settings. Ollama runs llama.cpp's own server, and the two were within 1% when started with the same command. llama.cpp was faster with four requests at once, because it starts four slots by default and Ollama starts one.

Recent findings suggest that ollama gives each parallel request its own full context. With four slots on a 24 GB card, that was 131,072 tokens, which pushed 16% of a 27B model onto the CPU. A smaller context may avoid that, but this test did not measure it.

In a recent development, when many requests arrive together. At 32 requests, vLLM produced 2.5 times the output of llama.cpp with 32 slots and kept every first-word wait under a second. For one request at a time, llama.cpp was 5% faster and started in seconds instead of more than a minute.

Recent findings suggest that usually not. All four serve OpenAI-compatible endpoints under /v1, so you change the base URL and the model name.

#172207. TimeScope: How Long Can Your Video Large Multimodal Model Go?

📅 23 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1019 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

TimeScope: How Long Can Your Video Large Multimodal Model Go?

📅 23 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that timeScope is an open-source benchmark designed to measure how well vision-language models understand long videos.
  • Recent findings suggest that recent advances in multimodal AI have produced models claiming to understand hour-long videos.
  • Text benchmarks such as HELM and RULER have exposed the fragility of long-context claims, showing that models often struggle when tasks demand more than simple retrieval, like reasoning or aggregation at long context lengths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that timeScope is an open-source benchmark designed to measure how well vision-language models understand long videos. By adding short “needle” clips into videos ranging from 1 minute to 8 hours, it evaluates three skills:.

Recent findings suggest that recent advances in multimodal AI have produced models claiming to understand hour-long videos. This trend mirrors progress in long-context language models, which excel at reasoning over lengthy text. Following this, vision-language systems now advertise context windows that can handle thousands of frames. But these claims require a closer look: do these models truly demonstrate understanding of the sequence of events? Are they limited to surface-level retrieval \ recognition? It's crucial to ask if their capabilities are being overstated.

Text benchmarks such as HELM and RULER have exposed the fragility of long-context claims, showing that models often struggle when tasks demand more than simple retrieval, like reasoning or aggregation at long context lengths. In the video domain, however, we're still playing catch-up. The most common test, Video Needle in a Haystack (VideoNIAH), injects static images as "needles" into videos, effectively measuring visual search rather than true temporal dynamics. As a result, even top-tier models advertising massive frame capacities are rarely trained beyond ~256 frames and see sharp drops on benchmarks like Video-MME when pushed further.

This measurement gap leaves us wondering: What does it really mean for a model to "understand" long videos? To address this, we're excited to introduce TimeScope, a new open-source benchmark hosted on Hugging Face. TimeScope probes the limits of long-video capabilities by inserting several short (~5-10 second) video clips—our "needles"—into base videos ranging from 1 minute to 8 hours. With three distinct task types, it evaluates not just retrieval but synthesis, localization, and fine-grained motion analysis, providing a more holistic view of temporal comprehension.

The promise of long-video AI is transformative — enabling agents to summarize hours of footage, detect subtle anomalies, and answer complex questions about extended narratives. Integrated into robotics, these models could analyze prolonged operations, adapt in real time, and push autonomous decision-making. Just as powerful is the vision of a personal assistant that understands daily life and offers continuous, actionable feedback.

In a recent development, in practice, this leads to overstated capabilities. Models might claim to process 10,000+ frames, but training data often caps at 256 frames per clip, leading to degraded performance on longer inputs. We've seen this in evaluations where increasing frame sampling rates tanks accuracy on tasks requiring temporal insight.

TimeScope flips the script by emphasizing three pillars of long-video understanding:.

TimeScope’s key idea is using short video clips as “needles,” and instead of just spotting the needle, it pushes models to deeply understand the whole video. We start with a long base video (e.g., a documentary, lecture, or ambient footage) and insert one or more hand-curated short video needles (5-10 seconds each) at random positions. These needles contain the key information needed to solve the task, forcing models to process the entire input without shortcuts like sparse sampling.

According to recent reports, figure 1: Overview of TimeScope's needle insertion process. A long base video (1 min to 8 hours) serves as the haystack, into which we splice short video needles (~5-10 seconds). Tasks require detecting, synthesizing, or analyzing content from these needles, embedded at varying depths.

We evaluate across three needle types, each targeting a different aspect of long-video comprehension:.

This tests basic retrieval and understanding of a localized event. Questions are put so that sampling a relevant frame from the needle should suffice—like asking about a shorter part in a longer video.

Example:What mode of transportation is shown in the video?

It has been revealed that here, we embed multiple text-based needles (e.g., 2-4 short clips displaying "secret words" via on-screen text) at different points in the video. The model must identify all words and report them in chronological order, simulating tasks like extracting timestamps or key facts from dispersed scenes. This requires scanning the full timeline and understanding relative positioning.

Industry observers note that for questions focusing on motion or sequences within a short clip, single-frame sampling won't cut it—the model needs to perceive dynamics across frames. This probes whether long-context handling preserves temporal fidelity.

Example:How many times did the man swing his axe? (a) one (b) two (c) three (d) four (e) five (f) six.

With different video lengths and varying needle placements, TimeScope measures how much video a model can really handle—and reveals that performance drops as the video gets longer.

To kick things off, we ran TimeScope on a suite of leading vision-language models, from open-source favorites to the juggernauts like Gemini 2.5-Pro. The results underscore the benchmark’s value: even models that claim to handle long videos well still struggle with real long-video tasks. These findings reveal clear patterns—performance cliffs around certain durations, strengths in static retrieval versus weaknesses in motion analysis—and pave the way for targeted improvements in model training. For detailed results and visualizations, check out our Hugging Face Space embedded above.

Sources indicate that model size isn’t everything. Qwen 2.5-VL 3B and 7B, as well as InternVL 2.5 models at 2B, 4B, and 8B parameters, exhibit nearly indistinguishable long-video curves to their smaller counterparts. All of them plateau at roughly the same context length, showing that simply scaling parameters does not automatically grant a longer temporal horizon.

In a recent development, gemini 2.5-Pro is in a league of its own. It is the only model that maintains strong accuracy on videos longer than one hour.

According to recent reports, trade-offs across tasks matter. Qwen 2.5-VL shines in the Information-Synthesis (OCR) task—identifying and ordering dispersed text snippets—yet it falls behind on Fine-Grained Temporal Perception, where precise motion counting is required.

TimeScope demonstrates that “hour-long video understanding” is still more slogan than reality. By revealing where even state-of-the-art models stumble on temporal reasoning, information synthesis, and motion perception, the benchmark invites us to rethink how we train and evaluate multimodal systems.

We hope this benchmark helps the community make steady, measurable progress toward models that better understand video over time.

We are open-sourcing all components of TimeScope:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home Office needs more time with the PNC, which began life more than 50 years ago.

Industry observers note that * Updated to add: A source close to the matter told The Register there is an agreement in place for support of the database software, however the Home Office would not comment. We first asked about the support contract several days prior to the publication of this article. The Register has filed a Freedom of Information request to compel the government to clarify the matter.*The UK’s Home Office has been unable to provide evidence to show how the Police National Computer (PNC) is getting vendor support for three years or more after it missed another deadline to decommission the aging crime-fighting system first introduced in 1974.

The PNC was first released in 1974, when Tom Baker began his iconic role playing Doctor Who, and has seen the tenure of 26 UK Home Secretaries, surviving multiple efforts to replace it.

It has been revealed that A notice in December 2024 stated that the Home Office was "focused on the development and adoption of the Law Enforcement Data Service (LEDS) products to replace existing PNC capability across all police forces and other non-policing PNC consumers, enabling the retirement by March 2026 (the point at which PNC support will expire)." We understand that PNC support refers to the Fujitsu support contract for the mainframe, which is housed in north London. Support for the Software AG database on the mainframe OS (BS2000) ran out at the end of 2024. So the database holding the crucial police data remains out of standard support and potentially will stay that way until 2027.The decommissioning date for the PNC had already been pushed back by the need to delay and "reset" the LEDS in 2020. The Home Office launched its successor, National Law Enforcement Data Service, in 2016, and planned to finish the new system by 2020 at a cost of £671 million.

The Home Office told The Register this week that it needed more time, and it aimed to begin decommissioning the system from March 2027, raising questions over how it would be supported.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "We are modernizing policing systems to adapt to evolving challenges, including rolling out the LEDS to replace the Police National Computer.

"While LEDS is already operational, we are continuing to run the legacy Police National Computer system to support the operational needs of all UK police," they said.

Officials said the PNC would remain available throughout the transition and would only be disconnected when police forces have confirmed that they no longer need it.

Industry observers note that earlier this month, in a written response in the House of Lords, Lord Hanson of Flint, a junior minister, said the PNC might be required until early 2028. Some LEDS services were already live and the program was "targeting completion of the remaining development, adoption and readiness activity in early 2027 as we prepare for our final stages for LEDS deployment before retiring the PNC," he said.

Industry observers note that "Once the transition of all police people to the LEDS has been completed and policing has confirmed that the PNC is no longer required, the system will be disconnected and decommissioned. The decommissioning process is expected to take place between late 2027 and early 2028," he noted.

It has been revealed that according to the National Audit Office (NAO), the PNC is the most important national policing information system in the UK. It serves front-line officers from all 45 local police forces, as well as by 127 other organisations that need to access its data. In 2019-20, the police searched or updated the PNC 133 million times.

The ongoing delay to the decommissioning of the PNC raises questions about how — and whether — it is being adequately supported.

The PNC is sited at a datacenter in Hendon, North London, and is based on a Fujitsu BS2000/OSD SE700-30 mainframe, but this is technology originally developed by German engineering outfit Siemens inherited by Fujitsu when it acquired the data processing division of that company.

It was the subject of controversy in 2021 when an error led to the accidental loss of 413,000 records of police evidence from the system, the result of a scripting error in code designed to weed out records targeted for deletion, although the lost data was eventually recovered.

It has been revealed that in 2022, Fujitsu — the Japanese tech giant at the center of the Post Office Horizon scandal — was awarded a £48 million ($56.6 million) renewed contract for support and maintenance of the PNC after no other companies tendered for the work. The contract was set to expire in March 2026.

In its 2021 report, NAO mentioned the Fujitsu mainframe computer used by the PNC would reach the end of its supported life by 31 December 2021.

"The Software AG database used by the PNC is only supported on the Fujitsu mainframe until 31 December 2023. The Department has an option to extend the contract for this support for a further 12 months but it has not yet agreed this with the supplier. If [the replacement system] is not ready, the PNC will need to be moved off the mainframe onto a supported operating system from 2025 or run unsupported," the report mentioned.

However, at the time, the Home Office told the NAO it had decided to accept the risk of running the PNC without support for the database for 12 months after December 2024. "This would leave the PNC at higher risk of disruption for at least a year, although the Department's view is that the actual risk profile is low because of the mitigation actions put in place," the report stated [PDF].

It added that moving the PNC to a latest operating system could take three years and Home Office estimated that it will cost at least £30 million, including the cost of rewriting code for the new OS.

A report from the Public Accounts Committee later in November 2021 mentioned: "The team that maintains the PNC is under-resourced and several staff are nearing retirement… The Department currently intends to run this piece of critical national infrastructure without full manufacturer support for the database after 2024, meaning it will not have that support for at least a year, though the Department plans to provide in-house support instead.".

According to recent reports, unless the Home Office has come up with another plan in the meantime, it is set to extend that out-of-support period to around three years. It has been offered the opportunity to provide additional comment. ®.

Tech Report: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking

📅 25 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reduce Parquet file upload and download times on Hugging Face Hub by leveraging the fresh Xet storage layer and Apache Arrow’s Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) feature enabling more efficient and scalable data workflows.
  • According to recent reports, TL;DR: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) is now available in PyArrow and Pandas, enabling efficient deduplication of Parquet files on content-addressable storage systems like Hugging Face's Xet storage layer.
  • Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format that is widely used in the data engineering community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reduce Parquet file upload and download times on Hugging Face Hub by leveraging the fresh Xet storage layer and Apache Arrow’s Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) feature enabling more efficient and scalable data workflows.

According to recent reports, TL;DR: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) is now available in PyArrow and Pandas, enabling efficient deduplication of Parquet files on content-addressable storage systems like Hugging Face's Xet storage layer. CDC dramatically reduces data transfer and storage costs by uploading or downloading only the changed data chunks. Enable CDC by passing the use_content_defined_chunking argument:.

Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format that is widely used in the data engineering community.

As of today, Hugging Face hosts nearly 21 PB of datasets, with Parquet files alone accounting for over 4 PB of that storage. Optimizing Parquet storage is therefore a high priority. Hugging Face has introduced a fresh storage layer called Xet that leverages content-defined chunking to efficiently deduplicate chunks of data reducing storage costs and improving download/upload speeds.

Industry observers note that while Xet is format agnostic, Parquet's layout and column-chunk (data page) based compression can produce entirely different byte-level representations for data with minor changes, leading to suboptimal deduplication performance. To address this, the Parquet files should be written in a way that minimizes the byte-level differences between similar data, which is where content-defined chunking (CDC) comes into play.

Let's explore the performance benefits of the new Parquet CDC feature used alongside Hugging Face's Xet storage layer.

For demonstration purposes, we will use a manageable sized subset of OpenOrca dataset.

Since pyarrow>=21.0.0 we can use Hugging Face URIs in the pyarrow functions to directly read and write parquet (and other file formats) files to the Hub using the hf:// URI scheme.

According to recent reports, we can see that the table has been uploaded entirely (total bytes == total transfer) as fresh data because it is not known to the Xet storage layer yet. Now read it back as a pyarrow table:.

Note that all pyarrow functions that accept a file path also accept a Hugging Face URI, like pyarrow datasets, CSV functions, incremental Parquet writer or reading only the parquet metadata:.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of the content-defined chunking feature, we will try out how it performs in case of:.

Recent findings suggest that while this use case sounds trivial, traditional file systems do not deduplicate files resulting in full re-upload and re-download of the data. In contrast, a system utilizing content-defined chunking can recognize that the file content is identical and avoid unnecessary data transfer.

We can see that no new data has been uploaded, and the operation was instantaneous. Now let's see what happens if we upload the same file again but to a different repository:.

The upload was instantaneous again since deduplication works across repositories as well. This is a key feature of the Xet storage layer, allowing efficient data sharing and collaboration. You can read more about the details and scaling challenges in the From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub blog post.

First write out the original and changed tables to local parquet files to see their sizes:.

Now upload them to Hugging Face to see how much data is actually transferred:.

We can see that only the new columns and the new parquet metadata placed in the file's footer were uploaded, while the original data was not transferred again. This is a huge benefit of the Xet storage layer, as it allows us to efficiently add new columns without transferring the entire dataset again.

Same applies to removing columns, as we can see below:.

To have a better understanding of what has been uploaded, we can visualize the differences between the two parquet files using the deduplication estimation tool:.

Sources indicate that adding two fresh columns mean that we have unseen data pages which must be transferred (highlighted in red), but the rest of the data remains unchanged (highlighted in green), so it is not transferred again. Note the small red area in the footer metadata which almost always changes as we modify the parquet file. The dedup stats show / = where smaller ratios mean higher deduplication performance.

Also visualize the difference after removing a column:.

Since we are removing entire columns we can only see changes in the footer metadata, all the other columns remain unchanged and already existing in the storage layer, so they are not transferred again.

Recent findings suggest that another common use case is changing the column types in the table e.g. to reduce the storage size or to optimize the data for specific queries. Let's change the question_length column from int64 data type to int32 and see how much data is transferred:.

It has been revealed that again, we can see that only the upcoming column and the updated parquet metadata were uploaded. Now visualize the deduplication heatmap:.

Recent findings suggest that the first red region indicates the new column that was added, while the second red region indicates the updated metadata in the footer. The rest of the data remains unchanged and is not transferred again.

We are going to append new rows by concatenating another slice of the original dataset to the table.

Now check that only the newly introduced rows are being uploaded since the original data is already known to the Xet storage layer:.

It has been revealed that since each column gets fresh data, we can see multiple red regions. This is due to the actual parquet file specification where whole columns are laid out after each other (within each row group).

In a recent development, here comes the difficult part as insertions and deletions are shifting the existing rows which lead to different columns chunks or data pages in the parquet nomenclature. Since each data page is compressed separately, even a single row insertion or deletion can lead to a completely different byte-level representation starting from the edited row(s) to the end of the parquet file.

This parquet specific problem cannot be solved by the Xet storage layer alone, the parquet file itself needs to be written in a way that minimizes the data page differences even if there are inserted or deleted rows.

Let's try to use the existing mechanism and see how it performs.

Also visualize both cases to see the differences:.

We can see that the deduplication performance has dropped significantly (higher ratio), and the deduplication heatmaps show that the compressed parquet files are quite different from each other. This is due to the fact that the inserted and deleted rows have shifted the existing rows, leading to different data pages starting from the edited row(s) to the end of the parquet file.

In a recent development, we can solve this problem by writing parquet files with a upcoming pyarrow feature called content-defined chunking (CDC). This feature ensures that the columns are consistently getting chunked into data pages based on their content, similarly how the Xet storage layer deduplicates data but applied to the logical values of the columns before any serialization or compression happens.

The feature can be enabled by passing use_content_defined_chunking=True to the write_parquet function:.

Pandas also supports the new feature:.

Let's visualize the deduplication difference before and after using the Parquet CDC feature:.

It has been revealed that looks much better! Since the proof of the pudding is in the eating, let's actually upload the tables using the content-defined chunking parquet feature and see how much data is transferred.

Note that we need to upload the original table first with content-defined chunking enabled:.

The uploaded data is significantly smaller than before, showing much better deduplication performance as highlighted in the heatmaps above.

Important to note that the same performance benefits apply to downloads using the huggingface_hub.hf_hub_download() and datasets.load_dataset() functions.

In a recent development, there are cases depending on the reader/writer constraints where larger or smaller row-group sizes might be beneficial. The parquet writer implementations use fixed-sized row-groups by default, in the case of pyarrow the default is 1Mi rows. Dataset writers may change to reduce the row-group size in order to improve random access performance or to reduce the memory footprint of the reader application.

Changing the row-group size will shift rows between row-groups, shifting values between data pages, so we have a similar problem as with inserting or deleting rows. Let's compare the deduplication performance between different row-group sizes using the parquet CDC feature:.

According to recent reports, datasets are often split into multiple files to improve parallelism and random access. Parquet CDC combined with the Xet storage layer can efficiently deduplicate data across multiple files even if the data is split at different boundaries.

Let's write out the dataset with three different file-level splitting then compare the deduplication performance:.

Even though we uploaded the dataset with three different sharding configurations, the overall upload size would be barely larger than the original dataset size.

So far we've used PyArrow, let’s explore using the same CDC feature with Pandas by downloading, filtering then uploading the dataset with the content-defined chunking feature enabled:.

Industry observers note that since Parquet CDC is applied at the parquet data page level (column chunk level), the deduplication performance depends on the filter's selectivity, or rather the distribution of the changes across the dataset. If most of the data pages are affected, then the deduplication ratio will drop significantly.

More details about the feature can be found at:.

It has been revealed that we explored the performance benefits of the upcoming Parquet content-defined chunking feature used alongside Hugging Face's Xet storage layer. We demonstrated how it can efficiently deduplicate data in various scenarios making parquet operations faster and more storage-efficient. Comparing to traditional cloud storage solutions, the Xet storage layer with Parquet CDC can significantly reduce data transfer times and costs.

Migrate your Hugging Face repositories from Git LFS to Xet to benefit from this here: https://huggingface.co/join/xet.

Does the Hugging Face Xet Storage also work on top of (self-hosted) Minio?

@sfkeller Not today, but the underlying technology is open source and we're in the process of documenting the backend! We initiative to release a Xet protocol later this year, which would open up the possibility to build for other backends as well. cc @rajatarya.

According to recent reports, this is great! I will look forward to the release of Xet protocol.

I hope it is written in Rust :).

Protocol + Format will be documentation, but there is the hf-xet implementation in Rust with xet-core.

I love YouTube on TV, but we desperately need better watchlist controls

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life.
  • Aside from my YouTube watchlist gripes, it’s no secret that moving from a web browser to the TV is ultimately still a frustrating experience.
  • Lots of things I love about watching videos on my laptop or PC just don’t translate well to when I’m sat on my sofa holding a remote trying to find something to watch after wrapping up for the day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life. Google’s premier streaming app has too many issues with resurfacing content; in my opinion, this is now a major problem that needs to be fixed.

Aside from my YouTube watchlist gripes, it’s no secret that moving from a web browser to the TV is ultimately still a frustrating experience.

Lots of things I love about watching videos on my laptop or PC just don’t translate well to when I’m sat on my sofa holding a remote trying to find something to watch after wrapping up for the day. One thing I’m getting annoyed with is how YouTube scales on TV and Android TV boxes because you’re given less choice and arguably poorer recommendations for content due to the constraints in place.

According to recent reports, understandably, you can’t compress the layout too much on a TV as you’re typically sat a few feet away and all aspects of the interface need to be legible. I would still like to tweak it, though, if that were possible.

Industry observers note that maybe we could get proper sections for content, like how Netflix and other streaming platforms offer categorized areas where you can search for “comedy” or “horror”. I’m almost certain that, with Google’s insane investment and massive AI push, where every video is already analyzed hundreds of times, that wouldn’t be too difficult to do.

The problem now is that the sidebar menu is just too broad. Gaming covers basically everything. Then each line of videos accounts for one title, but requires search and previous watch data to populate. I find myself often fighting with recommendations on my TV, whereas on desktop it’s not as much of a problem.

That leads me to my biggest problem with YouTube, and it’s the, frankly, embarrassing watchlist or “Watch later” controls.

In a recent development, I can’t fault that it works, but right now the watchlist function is like something out of the early 2000s due to the lack of flexibility that I touched on above. As my YouTube consumption has increased 20x over the past four or five years, managing what I want to come back to or might have missed the first time around is starting to become a bit of a chore.

I’ve tried using playlists to save things, but things get messy very quickly because of how cumbersome it is to a) create a playlist on TV and b) how playlists are organized by default.

It has been revealed that google TV isn’t perfect, but it’s where I keep my biggest TV and movie watchlist outside of YouTube. Yes, YouTube is mostly for user-generated content, but I would take something as basic as Google TV’s interface baked into YouTube somehow. Add in categorization and auto-clear.

The Watch Later section has become an unwieldy place that I never really want to go unless I desperately have to. I’m constantly losing videos that I hoped to come back to or have an affinity for.

Videos don’t clear automatically, nor do you know when they were added. Yes, I’ll give credit that you can sort by a few options, but that’s the bare minimum. The process of moving things around is slow and takes multiple taps. Watch Later is also hidden compared to other services. It’s under your account, then beneath “Liked videos,” which is below any you may have uploaded yourself.

On a TV, the process is so annoying I just avoid it altogether. You go to the sidebar menu > Library > Watch later. It should be front-and-center on a TV. It’s almost unforgivable in my eyes because even your watch history is given greater prominence. I simply cannot understand that decision.

I’m not always a huge fan of AI being shoehorned into apps and services, but this is one of those areas that has been left to rot for a while and could get a major uplift from adding in a little bit of Gemini. Even if it were just an enhanced search function or more tools for organizing.

With YouTube TV effectively taking over regular broadcast television and being the world’s biggest streaming platform, I’m shocked by how so many areas of the platform remain in a consistently neglected state.

A little bit of spit and polish, and maybe I’ll start using this section again. For now, though, I’ll stick to texting myself links of stuff I want to watch. The ball is in your court, Google.

#172201. Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (910 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theregister ↗ Open Full Page

Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple, Google, and Microsoft called out for failing to provide developers with adequate AI agent controls.
  • Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns.
  • Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal President Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple, Google, and Microsoft called out for failing to provide developers with adequate AI agent controls.

Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns.

Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal President Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private.

"Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post.

It has been revealed that "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.".

The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private.

Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text.

Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents.

Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system.

"We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said.

"Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are right now unable to implement these protections on macOS.".

Recent findings suggest that apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately.

Sources indicate that with macOS 27.3, at the moment in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs.

"As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple noted when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.".

Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers.

Recent findings suggest that while Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri highlights that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome.

AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants.

Recent findings suggest that amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses. United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others.

Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few.

The web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy.

Industry observers note that now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. After a year or two of agent vendors arguing for access to all digital data for the sake of personalization and context, the backlash has arrived. ®.

Industry observers note that correction: An earlier version of this article misstated Meredith Whitaker's title. She is the president of the Signal Foundation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are glad to announce a long-awaited quality-of-life improvement: the Hugging Face CLI has been officially renamed from huggingface-cli to hf!

According to recent reports, typing huggingface-cli constantly gets old fast. More importantly, the CLI’s command structure became messy as new features were added over time (upload, download, cache management, repo management, etc.). Renaming the CLI is a chance to reorganize commands into a clearer, more consistent format.

According to recent reports, we decided not to reinvent the wheel and instead follow a well-known CLI pattern: hf . This predictable grammar makes the Hugging Face CLI more ergonomic and discoverable, while also setting the stage for upcoming features.

To start playing with the upcoming CLI, you’ll need to install the latest huggingface_hub version:.

It has been revealed that and reload your terminal session. To test the install completed successfully, run hf version:.

Next, let’s explore the newly introduced syntax with hf --help:.

According to recent reports, as we can see, commands are grouped by "resource" (hf auth, hf cache, hf repo, etc.). We also surface hf upload and hf downloadat the root level since they’re expected to be the most-used commands.

To dive deeper into any command group, simply append --help:.

It has been revealed that if you are used to huggingface-cli, most commands will look familiar. The biggest change affects authentication:.

It has been revealed that online payments are an essential part of modern web applications. E-commerce platforms, subscription services, and online marketplaces all depend on payment gateways to process transactions and manage customer orders.

In a recent development, however, integrating a payment gateway involves more than adding a payment button or displaying a checkout form. Developers must ensure that payment requests are sent to legitimate providers, transaction information is validated correctly, and payment confirmations cannot be manipulated.

It has been revealed that fake payment gateways introduce another challenge. They can imitate legitimate payment interfaces, use copied checkout templates, and redirect customers to fraudulent websites. Even when a checkout page looks professional, its underlying implementation may not be trustworthy.

It has been revealed that for developers, understanding these risks is notable when designing payment workflows. This article explores common payment integration vulnerabilities and practical techniques for building secure checkout systems using JavaScript and Node.js.

A payment gateway connects an application with a payment processing service. It handles transaction requests and communicates payment results to the merchant's application.

A typical checkout process involves several components:.

A frontend checkout interface where customers review their orders.

A backend application that creates payment requests.

A payment provider that processes transactions.

A webhook endpoint that receives payment notifications.

A database that stores order and transaction information.

Attackers can target different parts of this process.

For example, a fraudulent website may copy the appearance of a legitimate checkout page while sending submitted information to an unauthorized server. Another approach involves manipulating payment requests or creating fake confirmation pages that make an unsuccessful transaction appear complete.

Recent findings suggest that these techniques are also relevant to marketplace fraud. An eBay scam can involve fraudulent payment requests and misleading transaction links, illustrating why developers need to consider payment security beyond the appearance of a checkout page.

The notable distinction is that a legitimate-looking interface does not establish that the payment request is reaching an authorized provider.

One of the first steps in reviewing a payment integration is checking where the application sends its payment requests.

Developers should inspect network requests using browser developer tools. The Network tab can reveal which domains receive requests when a customer opens the checkout page or submits a payment form.

Look for unexpected requests, unfamiliar domains, and scripts loaded from sources that are not part of the approved integration.

For example, a checkout application might load a payment script like this:.

The URL above is illustrative, not an actual payment provider.

Developers should compare the script URL and integration method with the provider's official documentation rather than trusting a URL simply because it appears familiar.

Reviewing external JavaScript dependencies.

Checking whether payment forms submit data to approved endpoints.

Inspecting redirects during checkout.

Confirming that HTTPS is used throughout the payment process.

Reviewing changes to payment-related scripts during development.

A Content Security Policy (CSP) can also restrict which domains are allowed to load scripts and receive certain types of requests.

These example domains must be replaced with the actual domains documented by the selected payment provider.

A carefully configured policy can reduce the risk of unauthorized scripts and unexpected form submissions.

A common mistake in payment development is trusting values submitted directly from the browser.

Consider an application where the frontend sends an order ID and payment amount to the backend.

An attacker could modify the amount before submitting the request. If the backend accepts that value without checking the original order, the application may create a payment session for an incorrect amount.

The safer approach is to retrieve the order from the database and calculate the amount on the server.

Here is a simplified Node.js example:.

Here, payment Gateway create Checkout Session() represents a provider-specific server-side SDK method.

The important part is that the backend retrieves the amount from its own database rather than accepting a price supplied by the customer.

Developers should also validate product IDs, quantities, discounts, currency, and order ownership before creating a payment session.

This prevents frontend manipulation from directly determining the final transaction amount.

Developers should avoid building payment processing around unverified scripts, copied templates, or unknown third-party services.

Instead, use official APIs and SDKs provided by established payment processors.

Recent findings suggest that A hosted checkout integration is one common option. The merchant's backend creates a payment session through the provider's API, and the customer is redirected to the provider's hosted checkout page.

This approach can reduce the amount of sensitive card information handled by the merchant's application.

However, developers still need to configure the integration correctly.

Store secret API keys in server-side environment variables or a secrets manager.

Never expose private credentials in frontend JavaScript.

Use the provider's official SDK where available.

Validate checkout session creation on the backend.

Restrict success and cancellation URLs to approved destinations.

Use HTTPS for application and payment communication.

Developers should also understand the difference between public and secret API credentials. Public keys may be designed for browser use, while secret keys must remain on the server.

The OWASP Third-Party Payment Gateway Integration Cheat Sheet provides additional guidance on securing payment requests, validating transaction details, and handling payment callbacks.

Payment providers often use webhooks to notify applications when transactions are completed, failed, or refunded.

However, webhook endpoints are publicly accessible URLs in many integrations. Without proper verification, an attacker may send a fabricated HTTP request that looks like a successful payment notification.

Developers should verify webhook signatures using the payment provider's official SDK.

Consider this simplified Node.js example:.

Sources indicate that the verify Webhook() method represents the signature verification functionality of a payment provider's SDK. It is not a universal Node.js method.

Recent findings suggest that the example also assumes that the provider's event contains the relevant order and transaction details. Developers should follow the provider's actual event schema and retrieve the authoritative payment status when required.

The application should never mark an order as paid simply because a customer has reached a success URL.

Instead, payment confirmation should depend on an authenticated provider notification or a server-side verification request.

Another key problem in payment development is duplicate processing.

Imagine a customer clicks the payment button twice because the first request takes too long. The application may create two payment sessions or attempt to charge the customer more than once.

Network interruptions and automatic retries can create similar situations.

Idempotency helps prevent these problems by ensuring that repeated requests with the same idempotency key do not create duplicate operations.

A simplified example using Node.js might look like this:.

The example uses a provider-specific idempotency option. Actual SDK syntax and key requirements vary between providers.

In a production application, developers should also store payment attempts in the database and enforce appropriate uniqueness constraints.

This helps maintain consistent transaction records even when requests are repeated or interrupted.

A payment integration should be tested beyond the normal successful checkout process.

Most established payment providers offer sandbox environments that allow developers to simulate transactions without charging real customers.

These environments are useful for testing different transaction scenarios.

A practical testing checklist includes:.

Missing or invalid webhook signatures.

Duplicate webhook notifications.

Network interruptions during checkout.

Incorrect order and transaction IDs.

Developers should also test whether the application handles provider downtime correctly.

For example, if the payment provider becomes temporarily unavailable, the application should not mark an order as completed or assume that the transaction succeeded.

Sources indicate that automated integration tests can help verify these scenarios before deployment. Monitoring payment failures, unexpected status changes, and repeated webhook errors can also help developers identify problems after release.

Security does not end when a payment integration goes live.

Developers should implement monitoring to identify unusual transaction patterns and unexpected changes in payment behavior.

Useful monitoring activities include:.

Recording payment attempts and transaction IDs.

Tracking failed payment requests.

Monitoring webhook signature verification failures.

Detecting repeated requests for the same order.

Alerting on unexpected order status changes.

Reviewing payment provider API errors.

However, logging must be implemented carefully.

Applications should never store card verification codes or expose secret API keys in application logs. Sensitive information should be excluded from debugging output, and access to transaction records should be restricted.

Developers should also follow the payment provider's security requirements and applicable PCI DSS obligations when handling payment data.

Detecting fake payment gateways and building secure checkout integrations requires more than checking whether a payment page looks legitimate.

Developers need to examine the complete transaction flow, validate payment information on the server, use official payment APIs, verify webhook signatures, and prevent duplicate transactions.

JavaScript and Node.js provide useful tools for implementing these security controls, but the reliability of a payment system ultimately depends on how its frontend, backend, database, and payment provider communicate.

Recent findings suggest that A well-designed checkout integration should verify every notable transaction before fulfilling an order. By following these development practices, teams can build payment systems that are easier to maintain, more reliable, and better protected against common payment manipulation techniques.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theregister ↗ Open Full Page

Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (628 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses.
  • On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information.
  • Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No financial details, but plenty of other clues.

Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses.

On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information.

Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand.

Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers.

“We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register. “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.”.

Mastercard previously stated that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program.

According to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker mentioned.

It has been revealed that it’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker.

Industry observers note that plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text,  and CRM ID format, Seker noted, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26.

“This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he mentioned. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.”.

The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published.

All three financial firms attributed the compromises to a third-party provider, and while nothing in the stolen files name the vendor, the timing matches up with a Qubole supply-chain campaign disclosed earlier this month by Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders and AI data security tech giant Sentra.

In that attack, which the threat hunters said began on October 14, cybercrims used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access dozens of downstream-customers’ environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets.

According to recent reports, N0n also claimed to have carried out this attack. “The timing fits the Qubole supply-chain campaign,” Seker said, adding that this is his company’s assessment, not a confirmed finding. "If it's right, Qubole would be the access path rather than the holder of the data, and the files point to a concierge-services operator behind the brands.”.

Recent findings suggest that qubole’s parent manufacturer Idera did not respond to The Register’s inquiries. The financial institutions declined to answer our questions about which provider(s) was compromised in the breach, and whether Qubole was the access path by which their customers’ data was exposed.®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, TL;DR: Trackio is a new, open-source, and free experiment tracking Python library that provides a local dashboard and seamless integration with Hugging Face Spaces for easy sharing and collaboration.
  • If you have trained your own machine learning model, you know how crucial it is to be able to track metrics, parameters, and hyperparameters during training and visualize them afterwards to better understand your training run.
  • Most machine learning researchers use specific experiment tracking libraries to do this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, TL;DR: Trackio is a new, open-source, and free experiment tracking Python library that provides a local dashboard and seamless integration with Hugging Face Spaces for easy sharing and collaboration. Since trackio is a drop-in replacement for wandb, you can get started with the syntax you already know!

If you have trained your own machine learning model, you know how crucial it is to be able to track metrics, parameters, and hyperparameters during training and visualize them afterwards to better understand your training run.

Most machine learning researchers use specific experiment tracking libraries to do this. However, these libraries can be paid, require complex setup, or lack the flexibility needed for rapid experimentation and sharing.

At Hugging Face, our science team has started using Trackio for our research projects, and we've found several key advantages over other tracking solutions:.

Easy Sharing and Embedding: Trackio makes it incredibly simple to share training progress with colleagues or embed plots directly in blog posts and documentation using iframes. This is especially valuable when you want to showcase specific training curves or metrics without requiring others to set up accounts or navigate complex dashboards.

Industry observers note that standardization and Transparency: Metrics like GPU energy usage are important to track and share with the community so we can have a better idea of the energy demands and environmental impacts of model training. Using Trackio, which directly gets information from the nvidia-smi command, makes it easy to quantify and compare energy usage and to add it to model cards.

Industry observers note that data Accessibility: Unlike some tracking tools that lock your data behind proprietary APIs, Trackio makes it straightforward to extract and analyze the data being recorded. This is crucial for researchers who need to perform custom analysis or integrate training metrics into their research workflows.

It has been revealed that flexibility for Experimentation: Trackio's lightweight design allows us to easily experiment with new tracking features during training runs. For instance, we can decide when to move tensors from GPU to CPU when logging tensors while training, which significantly improves training throughput when you need to track model/intermediate states without impacting performance.

In a recent development, ok then, so what is Trackio and how do you use it? Trackio is an open-source Python library that lets you track any metrics and visualize them using a local Gradio dashboard. You can also sync this dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, which means you can then share the dashboard with other customers simply by sharing a URL. Since Spaces can be private or public, this means you can share a dashboard publicly or just within members of your Hugging Face organization.

Eleven days after leaving Nvidia, Jensen Huang is back as president, CEO, and a board director. The board voted unanimously to reinstate him on Monday, saying it was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead following a series of meetings. It also stated input from senior levels of the US government left it confident that his reinstatement poses no national security risk.

I didn’t see this coming. Huang was dishonest to the public and to his board. He admitted to having affairs not only with an alleged Chinese spy, but also with an employee who directly reported to him. He is accused of facilitating the sale of Nvidia AI chips to companies like Megaspeed that knowingly purchased them with the intention of smuggling them into China, a contravention of US trade restrictions.

As recently as November 17th, the board chair, Harvey Jones, reiterated that the firm had no intention of bringing back Huang as CEO. But things changed promptly on Sunday as President Trump reportedly reassured the board that Huang’s reinstatement posed no security risk to US intelligence, something that the fresh Democratic-led Congress will be sure to test via repeated subpoenas in the new year.

As Huang walked into the atrium at Nvidia’s headquarters, staff gathered around to cheer his return, and he addressed the crowd by saying he would be a “better CEO the second time around,” as if 11 days of unemployment had given him sufficient time to evaluate his past behavior.

Sources indicate that nvidia’s stock was up over 30% on Monday, rebounding from a disastrous end to last week that wiped out $4 trillion in Nasdaq value. It’s hard not to see Huang’s return as a direct response to this short-term disruption, which also hinted at a much more serious correction in the stock market. Nvidia’s stock had already fallen 24% between the day Huang resigned and Friday’s crunch, and with looming regulation from Congress in 2027, a rudderless AI industry could have been disastrous for the US economy writ large.

Though things may appear to be back to normal, or as normal as possible given the insanity of the past couple of weeks, Huang has returned to a very different trade environment. While he was away, Nvidia’s board formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to investigate whether the company’s actions violated any US embargoes. And as part of Huang’s return, Nvidia has committed to hiring its first chief compliance officer, an executive who will ostensibly not report directly to the CEO.

Huang promises to be a better leader this time around, but to whom: his employees, his customers, or his shareholders? Because he appears to be a very different person to each of those groups.
